title: Chapter Seventeen:
leftColumn:
Chapter              S

                    Foreign            C

     T
         he glorious court of King Charlemagne attracts ambas-
         sadors and foreign knights from all over Europe and
         beyond. It is therefore important that game masters and
      players get a clear idea of who these strangers are, what they
      think and feel, and how they live and fight. In this chapter all
      major foreign cultures will be briefly discussed.
        Player-knights in Paladin are normally Franks, but in-
      spired game masters may allow alternative origins for their
      Player-knights. However, the information given here about
      game related characteristics is not quantified (with the exception
      of base Statistics), since it does not directly concern the Player-
      knights. This leaves game masters free to assign scores of their
      liking should the need arise.
        The sections on foreign culture are necessarily unfair.
      History is written by victors, and the descriptions below con-
      vey a strong Frankish bias. For example, the epics transform the
      splendid culture of Al-Andalus into the rather unsophisticated
      polytheistic pagan Moors.
        While some cultural evolution occurs (especially the
      adoption of Frankish customs, such as Knighthood, Chivalry
      and Romance), foreign armor and weapons do not evolve over
      time, as the Franks’ do. Many foreigners visit the Franklands to
      learn the virtues of knighthood, and they may have purchased
      or won current Frankish equipment, but the vast majority of
      the warriors in a foreign army are armed the same at the end of
      Charlemagne’s reign as at the beginning.
      Basques
      Names
      M
           en: Aitor, Anto, Arnalt, Centulo, Domingo, Eneko,
           Felix, Garcia, Garsan, Guillem, Iker, Inigo, Koldo,
           Lupus, Menant, Mikel, Otxoa, Pelayo, Peru, Remon,
      Sancho, Saubat, Urko, Xabier, Ximenes.
        Women: Garbina, Munia, Nekane, Oneca, Zutoia.
        Most male Basque names may be feminized by adding or
      changing the termination into -a: “Sancho” becomes “Sancha,”
      etc.

Seventeen:

 Cultures

  Appearance

     These stocky mountain folks are not very tall (–1 SIZ),
  but usually strongly-built, resilient (+1 CON) and dark-haired.
  Some have blue eyes, but all have a proud, penetrating look that
  puts foreigners ill at ease.
  Character
     The main Basques characteristic is their deep sense of inde-
  pendence and pride (Proud). They are very intolerant of authority
  (Arbitrary) and are often described as taciturn, treacherous and fickle
  (Deceitful). They obey only to their family and clan (Love [family]).
  Skills

     The Basques are widely known for their keen sight and
  hearing (Awareness), and for their numerous legends and super-
  stitions (Folk Lore, Faerie Lore).
  Relations with the Franks

     The Basque country is part of the duchy of Gascony and,
  as such, a part of the Frankish kingdom. However, when Duke
  Lupus of Gascony does homage to Charlemagne in 768, the
  Basques revolt and become a semi-independent nation whose
  leader pays only lip-service to the Franks.
     In 778, some local chieftains ally with the Moors at the
  slaughter of Roncevaux. At the death of their leader they once
  more pay homage to the Franks, but Charlemagne’s authority
  over the Basques remains weak at best.
  Chronology
    768 Duke Otxoa formally submits to Charlemagne, but in
      reality he remains more or less independent.
    771 Charlemagne captures Pamplona after the miraculous
      collapse of the city walls.
    778 The Basques support the Moorish ambush at Roncevaux,
      in which Duke Otxoa is killed.
    779 The new Duke, Orthez, pays homage to Charlemagne.
    806 The Franks quell a Basque revolt.
    812 Basque surrender after a second battle at Roncevaux.

title: Territory Warfare
leftColumn:
Territory

        The relatively small Basque country is located in the west-
      ern Pyrenees, with the River Ebro at its southern border. The
      western Pyrenees are inhospitable and mountainous, and can
      only be crossed in summer via the Roncevaux Pass. Even then,
      foreign travelers need a local guide.
        The mild sea climate provides enough rain water to irrigate
      the fertile green hills and mountain slopes. In the mountains,
      sudden fog and mist sometimes cover entire valleys.
      Places of Interest
      PaMPloNa

        This walled city is the only urban center in Basque Country.
      Pamplona is the seat of the duke, who lives in a wooden castle on
      the River Ebro.
      roNcevauX Pass
        This dangerous narrow pass on the border with Gascony is
      the only path by which to cross the western Pyrenees into Spain.

      Society
        Each Basque clan is ruled by a patriarch as far as military
      matters go. In case of conflict, he commands the warriors and
      leads all negotiations, consulting his kinsmen when necessary.
      The Basques have no ambition of conquering or subjugating
      their neighbors, but neither will they ever surrender to any for-
      eign people.
      Religion

        The Basques have been converted to Christianity only re-
      cently. Almost no ecclesiastic structure exists yet, as they have
      but a single bishop (in Pamplona), very few priests, and no mon-
      asteries at all.
        Not surprisingly, many pagan habits persist, such as gath-
      ering in mountain caves for goat sacrifices. Pagan Basques
      worship the weather gods Sugaar and Mari, who are supposed
      to live on mountain peaks. Hairy savages and gentle giants
      are said to inhabit the highest mountain regions as well, espe-
      cially where standing stones can be found. Another fabulous
      creature is the lamiak, a bird-footed nymph living near lakes
      or springs.
      Daily Life and Economy
        Pamplona, the seat of the duke, is the only Basque town.
      Basques live almost exclusively in poor mountain villages, where
      they practice sheep herding. Their way of life is completely
      self-sufficient, so they trade very little with the outside world.
        Women have a large role in Basque society. Indeed, fami-
      lies are based on matrilineal kinship. Women have a voice as es-
      teemed councilors and they may own property and land.
rightColumn:
Warfare

     Basques fight as mountain warriors. They have no cavalry,
  though they use their sturdy mountain ponies to carry equip-
  ment. They try to avoid open battle in the plains, preferring hit-
  and-run guerrilla warfare and ambushes, which allow them to
  take full advantage of the mountainous terrain.
  Standard Equipment
     Nobles: Leather armor (6 points), wooden shield (6
  points); spear, sword, dagger.
     Footmen: Animal skin armor (4 points), small wooden
  shield (4 points); spear or javelins, hand axe, bow or sling, dagger.

  Code  of Honor
     Knighthood, and chivalry especially, are unknown to the
  Basques. Their individual honor is based solely on family repu-
  tation. As a result, family feuds are numerous and long-lasting.
  The Basques are fundamentally hostile to any centralized power
  and are only superficially feudalized, having preserved many el-
  ements of their tribal society. Therefore, they often refuse to do
  homage or swear fealty to a Frankish overlord. When they do,
  such an oath has no value for them and they unhesitatingly break
  any promise that goes against the interest of their clan or family.
  Fortifications

     The Basques do not build castles. In case of impending
  trouble, wooden watch towers are used to inform the popula-
  tion, who may flee into hidden mountain caves if necessary.
  Bretons

  P
      ronunciation Note: When saying “Breton” or “Bretons”
      the stress falls on the second syllable.
      Names
     Men: Aquin, Conan, Dewi, Doret, Eon, Erispuë, Gael,
  Gwion, Karadeg, Morvan, Murman, Nominuë, Ronan, Salaoun,
  Yoann, Warok, Wiomarc’h.
     Women: Azenor, Enored, Erdisa, Madenn, Nolwenn,
  Tumed.

  Appearance
     The Bretons are a short (–2 SIZ), stocky (+1 CON), dark-
  haired, and rather unsophisticated people (–1 APP). The men
  can be recognized by their wild beards, and they often dress in
  simple black and white clothes.
  Character

    They originally came from Britain, from the end of the
    world. (…) That people, dishonest and pompous, have
    been in rebellion up to now, and lacking in goodwill. (…)

title: Relations with the Franks
leftColumn:
They take no thought for orphans, widows, churches. A
       man will lie down with his sister; one brother will rape
       another brother’s wife; everyone lives incestuously with
       everyone else; wickedness abounds. They live in briar
       patches and sleep in the woods and rejoice to live by theft
       in the manner of beasts. The force of justice claims no
       hall for itself with them, and the proper kinds of judg-
       ments escape them.
           — Ermold the Black, III
        The word “Breton” is derived from “brutal.” On the main
      Breton character traits are quite negative, with a reputation of
      being Deceitful, Lustful, Arbitrary and Cowardly, but they are
      also recognized as quite Energetic.
      Skills
        The Bretons live close to nature and know the secrets about
      the woods and its wild life (Folk Lore, Hunting), as well as many
      stories about the Other World (Faerie Lore). Almost all Bretons
      have a knack for music (Play Instruments).

      Relations with the Franks
        In the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign, the Bretons pay
      tribute in return for their independence. The converted Duke
      Samson of Brittany collects these taxes, but despite his title he
      does not rule over the Armorican peninsula. After the disaster
      at Roncevaux, the Breton leaders refuse to do homage and no
      longer send their traditional gifts, so Charlemagne orders the
      conquest of Brittany.
      Chronology

       753 Charlemagne made Duke of the Breton March.
       761 Charlemagne captures the city of Vannes.
       768 Roland made Count of the Breton March; Samson be-
          comes Duke of Brittany.
       779 Breton revolt. Wido, the new Count of the Breton
          March, ravages Brittany.
       785 The Bretons revolt and raid the Breton March.
       786 Charlemagne conquers Brittany and installs Salomon as
          its duke.
       789 Charlot made Duke of the Breton March.
       799 Count Wido suppresses a Breton revolt.
       804 Yet another Breton revolt.
       811 Wido reestablishes peace in the rebellious duchy.
      Territory

        The Armorican peninsula, also called Brittany, is divided
      into three regions: Leon in the west, Bro Weroc in the south-east
      and Domnonia in the north-east.
        The coastline consists of steep rocky cliffs, while the inte-
      rior is covered by vast swampy wastes and marshes, or by rug-
      ged wooded haunts filled with savage beasts and thorny under-
      brush. The landscape makes travel rather difficult, as roads, or
rightColumn:
even tracks, are almost completely absent. The Bretons use small
  boats to sail on rivers and along the rocky coast.
     The weather in Brittany is usually very humid, windy, and
  relatively cold compared to Neustria, much like the isles where
  the Britons live.
  Places of Interest
     Broceliande: A great primeval faerie forest which cov-
  ers almost the entire center of the peninsula. Inside these dark
  enchanted woods the weather is ever-changing (sudden mists,
  storms, or strange cold spot), and travelers invariably get lost.
     Carhaix: A medium wooden fortress, which serves as an
  ultimate refuge for the population in case of a foreign invasion.
     Carnac: A huge collection of standing stones surrounds
  the town, the remnants of a pagan army turned to stone by St.
  Cornelius.
     Dinard: A walled town on the estuary of the Rance, held
  by Prince Grimoart.
     Gardain (Brieuc): A strong stone castle dominates this
  small town, surrounded by a wide canal near the River Goët. The
  local ruler is Prince Doret.
     Menay: A small stone castle on the inland moors.

     Quidalet (Quimper): King Aquin holds this strong walled
  city, which is built on a peninsula surrounded by a large flood-
  ed ditch and flanked by a castle with a marble donjon tower
  (Aquin’s Tower). Many Frankish knights are held in shameful
  captivity in its Oreigle Prison.
  Society

    They do have a king, if it is right to call ‘king’ one who
     does not rule anyone.
       — Ermold the Black, III
     Nominally under the control of a Frankish duke, the
  Bretons recognize only the authority of their clan leaders, whom
  they continue to call kings. These chieftains often make war on
  each other, and the Franks do not hesitate to use these internal
  rivalries to their own advantage.
  Religion
     The Bretons are uneducated pagans, despite efforts to
  Christianize them. They worship a great variety of nature spirits
  at sacred sites, like the omnipresent dolmens or springs. Druids

segments.text:
They take no thought for orphans, widows, churches. A
       man will lie down with his sister; one brother will rape
       another brother’s wife; everyone lives incestuously with
       everyone else; wickedness abounds. They live in briar
       patches and sleep in the woods and rejoice to live by theft
       in the manner of beasts. The force of justice claims no
       hall for itself with them, and the proper kinds of judg-
       ments escape them.
           — Ermold the Black, III
        The word “Breton” is derived from “brutal.” On the main
      Breton character traits are quite negative, with a reputation of
      being Deceitful, Lustful, Arbitrary and Cowardly, but they are
      also recognized as quite Energetic.
      Skills
        The Bretons live close to nature and know the secrets about
      the woods and its wild life (Folk Lore, Hunting), as well as many
      stories about the Other World (Faerie Lore). Almost all Bretons
      have a knack for music (Play Instruments).

Relations with the Franks
        In the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign, the Bretons pay
      tribute in return for their independence. The converted Duke
      Samson of Brittany collects these taxes, but despite his title he
      does not rule over the Armorican peninsula. After the disaster
      at Roncevaux, the Breton leaders refuse to do homage and no
      longer send their traditional gifts, so Charlemagne orders the
      conquest of Brittany.
      Chronology

753 Charlemagne made Duke of the Breton March.
       761 Charlemagne captures the city of Vannes.
       768 Roland made Count of the Breton March; Samson be-
          comes Duke of Brittany.
       779 Breton revolt. Wido, the new Count of the Breton
          March, ravages Brittany.
       785 The Bretons revolt and raid the Breton March.
       786 Charlemagne conquers Brittany and installs Salomon as
          its duke.
       789 Charlot made Duke of the Breton March.
       799 Count Wido suppresses a Breton revolt.
       804 Yet another Breton revolt.
       811 Wido reestablishes peace in the rebellious duchy.
      Territory

The Armorican peninsula, also called Brittany, is divided
      into three regions: Leon in the west, Bro Weroc in the south-east
      and Domnonia in the north-east.
        The coastline consists of steep rocky cliffs, while the inte-
      rior is covered by vast swampy wastes and marshes, or by rug-
      ged wooded haunts filled with savage beasts and thorny under-
      brush. The landscape makes travel rather difficult, as roads, or

even tracks, are almost completely absent. The Bretons use small
  boats to sail on rivers and along the rocky coast.
     The weather in Brittany is usually very humid, windy, and
  relatively cold compared to Neustria, much like the isles where
  the Britons live.
  Places of Interest
     Broceliande: A great primeval faerie forest which cov-
  ers almost the entire center of the peninsula. Inside these dark
  enchanted woods the weather is ever-changing (sudden mists,
  storms, or strange cold spot), and travelers invariably get lost.
     Carhaix: A medium wooden fortress, which serves as an
  ultimate refuge for the population in case of a foreign invasion.
     Carnac: A huge collection of standing stones surrounds
  the town, the remnants of a pagan army turned to stone by St.
  Cornelius.
     Dinard: A walled town on the estuary of the Rance, held
  by Prince Grimoart.
     Gardain (Brieuc): A strong stone castle dominates this
  small town, surrounded by a wide canal near the River Goët. The
  local ruler is Prince Doret.
     Menay: A small stone castle on the inland moors.

Quidalet (Quimper): King Aquin holds this strong walled
  city, which is built on a peninsula surrounded by a large flood-
  ed ditch and flanked by a castle with a marble donjon tower
  (Aquin’s Tower). Many Frankish knights are held in shameful
  captivity in its Oreigle Prison.
  Society

They do have a king, if it is right to call ‘king’ one who
     does not rule anyone.
       — Ermold the Black, III
     Nominally under the control of a Frankish duke, the
  Bretons recognize only the authority of their clan leaders, whom
  they continue to call kings. These chieftains often make war on
  each other, and the Franks do not hesitate to use these internal
  rivalries to their own advantage.
  Religion
     The Bretons are uneducated pagans, despite efforts to
  Christianize them. They worship a great variety of nature spirits
  at sacred sites, like the omnipresent dolmens or springs. Druids
  no longer exist, and the Breton shamans are often no more than
  ignorant, superstitious story-tellers, whom even the Bretons
  themselves hold in rather low esteem.
  Daily Life and Economy

The people usually live in a small village on top of a hill,
  protected by a wooden palisade. Most houses are square wooden
  dwellings with low thatched roofs. The locals make a living from
  fishing and cattle herding. The whole of Brittany is quite poor,
  and trade with other lands almost non-existent.

title: Warfare
leftColumn:
Warfare

       They have often taken the path to our lands, but they do
       not go back to theirs unharmed.
           — Ermold the Black, III
        Bretons are mainly seasonal raiders. In battle they rely on
      light cavalry without horse-armor. Their favorite guerrilla tac-
      tic is to set traps and prepare ambushes for Frankish horsemen.
      Avoiding open battle with the superior Frankish troops, they
      often pretend to retreat and then turn around to attack. When
      cornered, the forest provides them with hidden routes which
      allow them to return unseen and attack their opponents in the
      back.
        Their few rules of honor are barbarian and as variable as the
      local weather. Bretons rarely ask a ransom for their prisoners, but
      they do accept the exchange of captured foes.
        Local chieftains build fortified barriers named guerches,
      which serve to block the waterways into the hinterland. These
      local magnates may live in a wooden or, rarely, stone tower. At
      best, the few Breton “kings” live in what they call a castle:
        [The king] lives in a place with woods on one side and a
       nice stream on the other, situated amidst hedges, trench-
       es and a swamp. Inside was a grand stone tower house
       that shone with the splendor of weapons whenever it hap-
       pened to be filled with different soldiers.
           — Ermold the Black, III
      Standard Equipment

        Nobles: Ring mail armor and round iron helmet (8 points),
      wooden shield (6 points); spear, iron sword, dagger; rouncy,
      courser.
        Horsemen: Leather armor (6 points); spear, dagger; rouncy.
        Footmen: Leather armor (6 points), wooden shield (6
      points); spear, dagger.
      Britons

      P
         ronunciation Note: When saying “Briton” or “Britons,”
         the stress is on the first syllable.
         Names
        Men: Ailward, Aldrich, Astulf, Bertric, Cenric, Coenwulf,
      Ecfrid, Edmund, Egbert, Gormond, Harold, Offa, Osbeorn,
      Sybald, Winfrid, Zerbin.
        Women: Alvina, Beorthred, Dara, Ethel, Maud, Mildredd,
      Nara, Rowena, Wilona.

      Appearance
        The people of the British Isles are much like the Franks,
      though more of them have red hair. Most nobles shave, though
      the ones from the isolated regions, such as Scotland or Cornwall,
      let their beards and hair grow. When not in armor, they wear
rightColumn:
checkered shirts and fine linen trousers, whereas the women
  dress in an elegant Romano-British style unique to the Isles.
  Character
     Britons are civilized gentlemen, much like the good Sir
  Astolf. The nobles try to follow the example of the Franks.
  As a people they are particularly lauded for their hard work
  (Energetic), sincerity (Honest) and their rather frugal way of life
  (Temperate).
  Skills

     The Britons are a sea-going nation of adventurers and mer-
  chants (Stewardship). They are known for their refinement
  and good manners (Courtesy), their sharp tongue and their
  particular sense of humor (Eloquence). The Britons are fervent
  Christians (Religion). Indeed, many monks and priests travel
  from the Isles to go and live in a monastery or an hermitage on
  the continent (Love [God]).
  Relations with the Franks

     The Britons take example from their respected Frankish
  brothers for many things. Charlemagne looks upon the British
  princes as his sons, and he is their natural ally against the Danes.
  Many British nobles send their sons to the continent to receive a
  proper knightly education at one of the Frankish courts.
  Chronology
    780 The Saracens raid the British coasts.
    789 Charlemagne wants to marry his son, Pepin the
      Hunchback, to Offa’s daughter; he refuses Offa’s count-
      er-proposal to marry his son, Ecfrith, to Charlemagne’s
      daughter Bertha.
    793 Danes sack the abbey of Lindisfarne in Northumbria.
    795 The Britons agree to pay a poll-tax to Charlemagne.
    796 King Offa’s death provokes a period of anarchy.
  Territory and Nations

     The term “Britons” is a generic name for all of the peoples
  inhabiting the British Isles, including the regions of Cornwall,
  Ireland, Mercia, Northumbria, Scotland, Wales and Wessex.
     The Isles are mostly covered by fertile green valleys and roll-
  ing hills. The few mountain ranges in Wales, Northumbria, and
  Scotland are not very high. The climate is often cheerless, foggy,
  and wet.
     The island’s ancient Roman roads have fallen somewhat in
  disrepair, but are still used by merchants and other travelers, in
  addition to the navigable rivers and streams. The major trading
  ports by which foreigners reach the Isles are Dover and London.
  Places of Interest

     Canterbury: A rich walled town has arisen around the fa-
  mous cathedral and scriptorium.
     Lindisfarne: A famous monastery near York.

title: Society
leftColumn:
London: The largest city of the British island and a pros-
      perous trading center. Within its Roman walls we find the
      White Tower, while Westminster Abbey is just outside the city.
        Offa’s Dyke: The Mercian king builds this long rampart in
      order to defend against Welsh raids.
        York: A great Roman city with a rich monastery and
      well-furnished library.
      Society

        As in Frankland, noblemen own the land and the feudal
      system produces knights and lords who rule over the peasant
      population. At the highest level, the British lands form a confed-
      eration, a so-called Heptarchy, where all seven territories remain
      independent but are allied in case of a foreign invasion. Each
      land is ruled by a clan chieftain, or king. The most powerful clan
      leader, usually the King of Mercia, is considered high-king of the
      Britons. At times, two clan leaders fight over the crown and it
      even happens that two rival kings exist at the same time, causing
      bloody internal strife.
      Religion
        The inhabitants of Britannia are faithful Christians. Many
      churches and cathedrals are being built, and the British monas-
      teries are renowned for their austere spiritual training, especially
      in the relatively isolated regions of Northumbria, Ireland and
      Scotland. In these religious establishments monks and copyist
      are preserving rare books, and exchanges with Frankish abbeys
      are frequent.
      Daily Life and Economy
        Apart from a few urban centers like London or York, most
      Britons live on the countryside in small farming communities.
      The peasants make their living from herding, especially sheep
      and goats. Along the coast, fishermen sail out daily on their small
      boats. In general, the Britons are not as rich as the Franks.
      Warfare

        British lords are often not as well equipped as their Frankish
      counterparts. They largely rely on levies of scantily armored
      footmen, with only a few knights to command them. The rare
      and expensive horses are saved for riding and pursuit, rarely rid-
      den in combat. In battle they make full use of archery.
        There is one point at which the Britons are superior to
      Charlemagne: their fleet is better equipped and organized,
      though still unable to rival the sea-borne Danes.
      Standard Equipment

        Nobles: Ring mail armor and iron helmet (8 points), wood-
      en shield (6 points); spear, sword, dagger; courser or charger.
        Horsemen: Leather armor and iron helmet (6 points),
      spear, sword, dagger; rouncy.
        Footmen: Leather armor and a leather cap (5 points),
      wooden shield (6 points); spear, dagger or short sword, bow.
rightColumn:
Code of Honor
     British nobles are generally honorable and follow the code
  of knighthood. Their word can be trusted.

  Fortifications
     Much like in Frankland, the British lords live in fortified
  manors or small wooden motte castles to which the local popu-
  lation may flee in case of attack, especially in the exposed coastal
  areas.

  Byzantines

  Names
  M
        en: Adrian, Alexander, Alexis, Aristakes, Bardas,
        Basil, Cecaumenos, Constantinos, Cosmas,
        Demetrios, Elias, Eumathios, Galien, Gregorias,
  Heracles, Isidore, Justinian, Kostas, Leo, Lysas, Manuel, Marcian,
  Melitas, Michael, Narses, Niketas, Nikephoros, Phocas, Petros,
  Sim (e) on, Staurakios, Tarasios, Theodose, Tiberios, Thoros,
  Xiphilin, Zacharias.
     Women: Aelia, Anastasia, Ariadne, Eudocia, Euphrosyne,
  Flacilla, Galla, Helena, Irene, Juliana, Licinia, Loukia, Macrina,
  Metrodora, Procopia, Scleraina, Sophia, Styliane, Thecla,
  Verina.
  Appearance
     Like all Mediterranean people, the Byzantines are slightly
  smaller and less robust than the Franks (–1 SIZ, –1 STR). They
  have long straight noses. They dress in elegant robes like the
  Romans, take good care of their looks and are found to be quite
  beautiful (+1 APP) and handy (+1 DEX).
  Character
     The Byzantines are known to be particularly Proud,
  Deceitful, Indulgent, and Suspicious of Franks. Still,
  Byzantines are a type of Christians (Love [God]). In the long
  and bloody wars against the Bulgars and the Persians, many

segments.text:
London: The largest city of the British island and a pros-
      perous trading center. Within its Roman walls we find the
      White Tower, while Westminster Abbey is just outside the city.
        Offa’s Dyke: The Mercian king builds this long rampart in
      order to defend against Welsh raids.
        York: A great Roman city with a rich monastery and
      well-furnished library.
      Society

As in Frankland, noblemen own the land and the feudal
      system produces knights and lords who rule over the peasant
      population. At the highest level, the British lands form a confed-
      eration, a so-called Heptarchy, where all seven territories remain
      independent but are allied in case of a foreign invasion. Each
      land is ruled by a clan chieftain, or king. The most powerful clan
      leader, usually the King of Mercia, is considered high-king of the
      Britons. At times, two clan leaders fight over the crown and it
      even happens that two rival kings exist at the same time, causing
      bloody internal strife.
      Religion
        The inhabitants of Britannia are faithful Christians. Many
      churches and cathedrals are being built, and the British monas-
      teries are renowned for their austere spiritual training, especially
      in the relatively isolated regions of Northumbria, Ireland and
      Scotland. In these religious establishments monks and copyist
      are preserving rare books, and exchanges with Frankish abbeys
      are frequent.
      Daily Life and Economy
        Apart from a few urban centers like London or York, most
      Britons live on the countryside in small farming communities.
      The peasants make their living from herding, especially sheep
      and goats. Along the coast, fishermen sail out daily on their small
      boats. In general, the Britons are not as rich as the Franks.
      Warfare

British lords are often not as well equipped as their Frankish
      counterparts. They largely rely on levies of scantily armored
      footmen, with only a few knights to command them. The rare
      and expensive horses are saved for riding and pursuit, rarely rid-
      den in combat. In battle they make full use of archery.
        There is one point at which the Britons are superior to
      Charlemagne: their fleet is better equipped and organized,
      though still unable to rival the sea-borne Danes.
      Standard Equipment

Nobles: Ring mail armor and iron helmet (8 points), wood-
      en shield (6 points); spear, sword, dagger; courser or charger.
        Horsemen: Leather armor and iron helmet (6 points),
      spear, sword, dagger; rouncy.
        Footmen: Leather armor and a leather cap (5 points),
      wooden shield (6 points); spear, dagger or short sword, bow.

Code of Honor
     British nobles are generally honorable and follow the code
  of knighthood. Their word can be trusted.

Fortifications
     Much like in Frankland, the British lords live in fortified
  manors or small wooden motte castles to which the local popu-
  lation may flee in case of attack, especially in the exposed coastal
  areas.

  Verina.
  Appearance
     Like all Mediterranean people, the Byzantines are slightly
  smaller and less robust than the Franks (–1 SIZ, –1 STR). They
  have long straight noses. They dress in elegant robes like the
  Romans, take good care of their looks and are found to be quite
  beautiful (+1 APP) and handy (+1 DEX).

     The Byzantines are known to be particularly Proud,
  Deceitful, Indulgent, and Suspicious of Franks. Still,
  Byzantines are a type of Christians (Love [God]). In the long
  and bloody wars against the Bulgars and the Persians, many
  of them develop a Hate [Bulgars] or Hate [Persians]. Though
  their luxurious way of life and frequent change of politics have
  somewhat diminished it, their Honor is generally still higher
  than their Love [family].

  very complex, but very efficient (Stewardship). To outsiders it

the arts of debate and persuasion (Eloquence) or even sophisti-
      cated theological arguments (Religion). Their empire has many
      islands, so most inhabitants have some skill as a navigator or sail-
      or. Another particularity is their fondness of the chariot races
      organized in great arenas.
      Relations with the Franks

       If a Frank is your friend, he is certainly not your neighbor.
           — Byzantine proverb
        The Byzantines dream of restoring the ancient Roman
      Empire, of which they pretend to be true heirs. They see them-
      selves as the guardians of classical and Roman civilization and
      the center of Christianity. They perceive the Franks as powerful
      barbarians. The Byzantines and Franks share two enemies: the
      Bulgars and the Saracens.
        Phase 1–2: As long as the Lombard exiles receive Byzantine
      support in their attempts to reconquer their lost Italian territo-
      ries, the Franks view Byzantium as a peaceful enemy.
        Phase 3–4: When Benevento finally submits and the
      Saracen pressure on Byzantium grows, the Franks are no lon-
      ger enemies, but become a sort of amiable rivals. This produc-
      es a half-hearted alliance and some marriage proposals, most of
      which are ultimately abandoned. Despite insistent Byzantine
      demands, Charlemagne refuses to declare war on the Persians.
      Worse, he is on friendly terms with the caliph.
      Chronology
       769 Voyage of Charlemagne to Jerusalem and
          Constantinople.
       775 Constantine V killed in battle by the Bulgars.
       776 The deposed khagan Telerig of the Bulgars flees to
          Byzantium and is baptized.
       780 Emperor Leo IV becomes obsessed with a votive crown
          from the treasury of St. Sophia. When he tries it on,
          boils break out on his head and he dies. His widow,
          Irene, becomes regent-empress for her 9-year-old son
          Constantine VI.
       781 Prince Constantine VI betrothed to the eight-year
          old princess Rothrud; a Byzantine Magister is sent to
          Frankland to teach the princess Greek language and
          customs.
       787 The betrothal between Constantine VI and Rothrud
          ends.
       790 An earthquake hits Constantinople. Civil war between
          Empress Irene and Thomas the Slav.
       791 The imperial army is defeated by the Bulgars.
       792 Constantine sends the Bulgar khagan a packet of horse
          manure to defy him.
       797 Constantine VI captured and blinded by his mother,
          who becomes basilissa (empress) herself.
       802 Empress Irene proposes to marry Charlemagne, but a
          Palace conspiracy in favor of Nikephoros deposes the
          Empress. Irene is sent into exile.

    811 Nikephoros sacks the Bulgarian capital, but is then
      killed in battle by the Bulgars (who make a drinking
      cup of his skull). His son, Staurakios, abdicates in favor
      of Michael Rangabe, then dies of wounds inflicted at
      Pliska.
  Territory
     Although the Eastern Roman Empire (now called the
  Byzantine Empire or simply Byzantium) is declining, it still
  covers a vast geographical area. To the east lies the thinly pop-
  ulated Anatolian mountain region, which has hot, dry summers
  and cold, wet winters. It is mainly used to pasture livestock. The
  rest of the empire (including Constantinople) consists of coastal
  plains with a mild climate, suitable for raising grain, vegetables,
  vines, and olives.
     Many different people live in all these regions, but they
  are all Byzantines. The mainland is divided into 6 themata (the
  equivalent of duchies). Apart from Constantinople, the most
  important cities are Tessalonica, Adrianople, Nicaea, Smyrna,
  Ephesus, Ancyra, Amorium, Attalia and Trebizond.
     The Byzantines hold power over many isles including Crete
  and Cyprus, and they have managed to cling to their Italian ter-
  ritories: Ravenna (seat of the exarch, the representative of the
  Byzantine Emperor in Italy), Venice and Istria in the north, the
  duchy of Calabria and Sicily in the south. These enclaves behave
  as if they are allies, rather than Byzantine possessions.
     To go to Byzantium via the Danube is virtually impossible
  because of the hostile Avars. Traveling by boat from Italy is the
  safest and easiest route.
  Places of Interest
     Constantinople: The famous and ancient capital of
  Byzantium is surrounded by impressive city walls and guard-
  ed by a thousand knights. Its fresh water is supplied by a great
  aqueduct. The marvelous palace of the Byzantine Emperor,
  called the Hieria, rotates around a huge central pillar and is
  ornamented with moving and singing statues. The inhabitants
  of Constantinople are very fond of chariot races which are or-
  ganized at the Hippodrome on special occasions. The city is
  the empire’s political, economic and cultural center, and it’s
  by far the largest and wealthiest city in Europe. The churches
  have golden roofs! Still, crime is almost unknown since the city
  guards maintain a very high level of vigilance. The capital har-
  bors a small minority of Jewish merchants.
  Society
     Once a powerful empire, Byzantium today is a giant with
  feet of clay. Although still extremely wealthy, the army is unruly
  and the leaders weak and decadent. Palace conspiracies and pop-
  ular revolts are quite frequent. The emperor (basileus) is assisted
  by ministers (logothetes), great nobles (patricians), and military

leftColumn:
leaders (strategoi). The palace guards are usually eunuchs; some
      have had their tongue cut out as well.
        When a prince wants to choose a wife, a bride show is held
      at court in order to find the most beautiful girl of the empire. To
      make rivals unfit for the office of basileus, they are castrated, have
      their eyes or tongues cut out, and are then sent to a monastery.
      Religion
        The Byzantines are Christians, but say mass in Greek in-
      stead of Latin. They venerate not only holy relics (of which they
      possess an impressive amount) but also images and idols, which
      is a heresy condemned by the pope of Rome. Their many monks
      and opulently-dressed priests aren’t chaste. The Byzantine Pope
      is called the Patriarch of Constantinople, and he is at the per-
      sonal service of the Basileus. The Byzantines often demand the
      aid of astrologers who can read the future in the stars, and of
      sorcerers who conjure up demons.
      Daily Life and Economy

        The Byzantines are appallingly wealthy and relatively ed-
      ucated. Their merchants operate in the Mediterranean Sea un-
      der the protection of the imperial fleet and carry considerable
      riches in spices, silks, gold and slaves. The main trade routes via
      land lead to Sericane, Persia and even Cathay. The Byzantines
      maintain a very efficient postal service used by the army and
      merchants.
      Warfare
        The Byzantines are constantly at war with the Huns
      from Bulgaria, the Persians (to whom they sometimes have to
      pay heavy tributes in return for peace), and the Saracens from
      Babylon. On the other hand, the Khazars (Circassians) are nat-
      ural allies against the Persians. Without declaring open war,
      Empress Irene starts to colonize deserted Slavic lands on the
      European mainland.
      Armies and  Tactics

        The Byzantine troops are a professional army, whose sala-
      ries are paid by the emperor. Armor and weapons are manufac-
      tured at state factories. They wear Roman-style uniforms and
      include many foreign mercenaries. They are well equipped, but
      have low morale and their war leaders often serve different in-
      terests. Moreover, the Byzantines often hire additional foreign
      mercenaries in the wars against the Bulgars or Slavs. Their army
      standard is the double-headed eagle.
        There are several army ranks, comparable to the Frankish
      ones: cataphract (knight), theme (vassal), tagmata (scara), droun-
      garios (banneret), turmarch (count), strategos (duke). Imperial
      tagmata are heavy cavalry units under the direct command of
      the basileus. They operate as body guards and are quartered at
      the palace in Constantinople.
        The Byzantines have a large fleet, which gets almost entirely
      destroyed in a civil war in 802–803. In sieges or naval battles, the

      at court in order to find the most beautiful girl of the empire. To
      make rivals unfit for the office of basileus, they are castrated, have
      their eyes or tongues cut out, and are then sent to a monastery.
      Religion
        The Byzantines are Christians, but say mass in Greek in-
      stead of Latin. They venerate not only holy relics (of which they
      possess an impressive amount) but also images and idols, which
      is a heresy condemned by the pope of Rome. Their many monks
      and opulently-dressed priests aren’t chaste. The Byzantine Pope
      is called the Patriarch of Constantinople, and he is at the per-
      sonal service of the Basileus. The Byzantines often demand the
      aid of astrologers who can read the future in the stars, and of
      sorcerers who conjure up demons.
      Daily Life and Economy

The Byzantines are appallingly wealthy and relatively ed-
      ucated. Their merchants operate in the Mediterranean Sea un-
      der the protection of the imperial fleet and carry considerable
      riches in spices, silks, gold and slaves. The main trade routes via
      land lead to Sericane, Persia and even Cathay. The Byzantines
      maintain a very efficient postal service used by the army and
      merchants.
      Warfare
        The Byzantines are constantly at war with the Huns
      from Bulgaria, the Persians (to whom they sometimes have to
      pay heavy tributes in return for peace), and the Saracens from
      Babylon. On the other hand, the Khazars (Circassians) are nat-
      ural allies against the Persians. Without declaring open war,
      Empress Irene starts to colonize deserted Slavic lands on the
      European mainland.
      Armies and  Tactics

The Byzantine troops are a professional army, whose sala-
      ries are paid by the emperor. Armor and weapons are manufac-
      tured at state factories. They wear Roman-style uniforms and
      include many foreign mercenaries. They are well equipped, but
      have low morale and their war leaders often serve different in-
      terests. Moreover, the Byzantines often hire additional foreign
      mercenaries in the wars against the Bulgars or Slavs. Their army
      standard is the double-headed eagle.
        There are several army ranks, comparable to the Frankish
      ones: cataphract (knight), theme (vassal), tagmata (scara), droun-
      garios (banneret), turmarch (count), strategos (duke). Imperial
      tagmata are heavy cavalry units under the direct command of
      the basileus. They operate as body guards and are quartered at
      the palace in Constantinople.

title: Relations with the Franks
leftColumn:
was a god, and Jupiter assumed Christ’s place; they paid
       him all sacred honors. This people were called Danes.
       They are also called Northmen by the Franks. They are
       fast, agile and well-armed. They inhabit the sea and seek
       out wealth by ship.
           — Ermold the Black, IV
      Skills

        They are the undisputed rulers of the sea, sailing as far as
      possible to trade their merchandise (Stewardship). They have a
      knack for exaggerated stories (Folk Lore, Faerie Lore), they excel
      in Swimming and other physical activities. On the other hand,
      Danes seem hardly inclined to learn any courtly skills apart from
      Gaming. They live by a moral code in which notions as courage,
      hospitality, and Love [family] are central.
      Relations with the Franks
        As allies of the Saxons the Danes are the enemies of the
      Franks, even though they rarely meet on the battlefield in the
      early years of Charlemagne’s reign. At the end of the Paladin
      chronology, though, the Danes become more and more aggres-
      sive, attacking the shores of Britannia first, later Frisia and even
      some northern Frankish coasts. Alcuin writes a lament about the
      Danish destruction of the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793:
       How painful to everyone was that day, when, alas,
       A pagan war band arrived from the ends of the earth,
       Descended suddenly by ship and came to our land,

       Despoiling our fathers’ venerable tombs of their finery
       And befouling the temples dedicated to God,
       And Sorech, the most pure vine of the divine Christ,
       Was suddenly gnawed by the teeth of foxes.
      Chronology

       757 King Pepin defeats the Danes. Prince Ogier is taken to
          Frankland as a hostage.
       781 Giants attack Denmark. Death of King Godfrid I. Sir
          Ogier’s half-brother Guyon becomes King Hemming I.
       793 The Danes pillage the abbey of Lindisfarne in
          Northumbria.
       810 The Danes make war on Slavs and sack Frisia. King
          Godfrid II is murdered. His successor, Hemming II,
          makes peace with the Franks.
       812 Civil unrest at the death of King Hemming II.
      Territory
       From the Western Ocean there stretches eastwards an
       arm of the sea of unknown length, nowhere exceeding a
       hundred miles in width, and much narrower in many
       places. Round this sea live many peoples. The Danes oc-
       cupy its northern shore and all its islands.
           — Einhard
rightColumn:
Denmark lies north of Saxony and is known as a land of
  cold and darkness. Monks describe it as the land of the Devil.
  Beyond Denmark are only inaccessible icy mountains in a land
  of eternal winter.
  Terrain Types
     A rather flat and fertile coastal landscape of sand dunes,
  melt-water plains, bogs, peat and sea marshes. The inner
  part of Denmark is covered with sloping forests. Beyond the
  Danish islands lie inhospitable icy mountains inhabited by
  trolls and giants.
  Travel

     To go to Denmark, it is easiest by boat or following the
  trade road through Saxony. Since no bridges exist, most rivers
  have to crossed by fording them (beware of cold shock and float-
  ing chunks of ice). In winter people use skis or sledges.
  Places of Interest
     Danevirke: Constructed by King Godfrid in 808, the
  Danevirke is an enormous fortified earthen rampart stretching
  40 km from coast to coast. It is intended to protect Danish raid-
  ers from Frankish pursuit, which is why it has only one entrance.
     Haithabu: A fortified merchant town, with the great gild-
  ed hall of the Danish king at its center.

  Society
     A single king rules over a society which is divided into class-
  es: nobles are called jarls, landowning freemen are carls, land-
  less serfs are thralls, and at the bottom of the social scale we find
  slaves, usually captured during raids in Slavonia, who wear iron
  bands around their necks.
     Groups of families together form clans, led by its most glo-
  rious member, usually a rich older jarl. Each clan holds annual
  assemblies: the landthings. These are popular meetings where
  free men unite under the leadership of powerful landholders.
  A law court is held, usually accompanied by a great market. On
  the highest level, the clan leaders meet at the allthing, under the
  supervision of the king himself. Legal disputes may be settled by
  ordeals, judicial duels or by paying wergild.
  Religion
     The chief landholders are also the priests of a pagan cult
  similar to that of the Saxons. Danes worship several Gods, such
  as Odin (magic, poetry), Tyr (war), Thor (thunder, home), Frey
  (weather, farming) and Freya (love, fertility). Shamans carve
  magic runes in bark, wood or stones. Their temples are out in
  the open fields. The dead are either cremated or buried in grave
  mounds along with valuable possessions.
     Skalds are the Danish poets and singers. They recite the
  laws of the land and sometimes act as independent itinerant
  judges. They sing of heroic deeds and the exotic creatures known
  to inhabit the North, such as mermaids, dragons, underground
  dwarfs and goblins.

title: Gascons
leftColumn:
Daily Life and Economy
        Apart from the capital, Haithabu, and Birka, there are no
      towns in Denmark. The Danes live in small villages, often on the
      coast. Chiefs live in a great wooden hall. Some rich Danes have
      more than one wife.
        Most Danes tend to their farms or sail out to go fishing,
      but they are also able seafaring merchants and pirates. Their fast
      longships cover great distances, all the way to the British Isles,
      Frankland and Slavonia. Sometimes smaller groups get permis-
      sion to navigate in the Frankish mainland via the Rhine, the
      Meuse and other rivers used as commercial routes. Instead of
      silver pieces, the Danes use hacksilver, cattle and barter.
       That region produces no useful fruit, but a multitude of
       beasts and cattle, horses (larger and more useful than
       those of other peoples); it produces much crystal and the
       most clear amber, hard like stones. (…) It is also very rich
       in iron.
           — Aethicus Ister

      Warfare
        At the end of the eighth century the coastlines of England
      and Frankland come under attack from Danish raiders. They
      even threaten the prosperous port of Dorestad. Their favorite

Daily Life and Economy
        Apart from the capital, Haithabu, and Birka, there are no
      towns in Denmark. The Danes live in small villages, often on the
      coast. Chiefs live in a great wooden hall. Some rich Danes have
      more than one wife.
        Most Danes tend to their farms or sail out to go fishing,
      but they are also able seafaring merchants and pirates. Their fast
      longships cover great distances, all the way to the British Isles,
      Frankland and Slavonia. Sometimes smaller groups get permis-
      sion to navigate in the Frankish mainland via the Rhine, the
      Meuse and other rivers used as commercial routes. Instead of
      silver pieces, the Danes use hacksilver, cattle and barter.

title: Warfare
leftColumn:
Chronology
       759 King Pepin declares war on Duke Waifer of Aquitaine.
       760 King Pepin liberates Septimania and installs Milo of
          Aiglent as the new Duke of Toulouse.
       768 King Pepin captures Duke Waifer, who dies soon after.
          His son Hunold escapes to Gascony.
       769 Duke Lupus of Gascony hands Hunold over to
          Charlemagne in return for peace. Aquitaine and Gascony
          come entirely under Frankish control. Charlemagne ap-
          points many Frankish abbots, counts and bishops.
       781 Coronation of Louis as King of Aquitaine.
       787 The Gascon Odalric captures his Visigothic rival, Duke
          Chorso of Toulouse.
       790 William Shortnose becomes Duke of Septimania.
       803 Heroic death of Duke Sevin, who saves King Louis’ life
          in Spain.
       806 Bego succeeds William as Duke of Septimania.
      Territory

        For detailed descriptions of Aquitaine and Gascony, see
      Chapter 14: Frankland.
      Society

        Gascon feudalism is somewhat different from what the
      Franks know. Indeed, many local magnates have no overlord
      and hold their land as a free fief, or allod. After the submission
      of Gascony in 768, Charlemagne continues this tradition and
      distributes allodial fiefs to local and Frankish nobles in order to
      secure their loyalty.
      Religion
        The Gascon people are Romanized and Christian, and if
      every town has a stone church with a bell, there are surprisingly
      few and relatively small monasteries. Unsurprisingly, many pa-
      gan beliefs, magic practices and superstitions are still very much
      alive in the remote outskirts of the two duchies.
      Daily Life and Economy

        Gascony used to be a more urbanized region, but during
      King Pepin’s wars against Aquitaine, and to a lesser degree
      Gascony, many towns were ravaged and their population fled
      to the surrounding countryside, leaving the urban centers
      abandoned.
        One notable characteristic of Gascon culture is that wom-
      en have more rights and play a more prominent role in public
      life than Frankish women. It is not unusual for a noble widow
      or sister of a deceased lord to govern his lands until a male heir
      comes of age.
        The once-prosperous lands and vineyards have been devas-
      tated by the many years of war and stubborn resistance against
      King Pepin. Many roads are in disrepair and there is almost no
rightColumn:
external commerce left, so the people depend on the local econo-
  my centered around the rural manors, which they still call villas,
  in much the same way as the Franks.
  Warfare

     Gascons fight primarily as infantry or javelin-using light
  cavalry skirmishers. They have neither stirrups nor saddles,
  but are skillful horsemen nevertheless. Under Charlemagne,
  the Gascons often serve as mercenaries in feuds. In battle, their
  favorite cavalry tactic consists of repeated attack followed by
  feigned retreat.
  Equipment
     Nobles: Ring mail armor (8 points), shield (6 points);
  spear, sword, dagger; rouncy and courser.
     Horsemen: Ring mail armor (8 points); spear, bow, dagger;
  rouncy.
     Footmen: Leather armor and skullcap (5 points), wooden
  shield (6 points); spear or javelins, dagger.

  Code of Honor
     Gascon knights are men of honor, though not particularly
  noted for their extreme valor nor their sense of loyalty. As said,
  they often hold allodial lands and therefore recognize no liege,
  even though they swear an oath of fidelity to the king.

  Huns

  Names

        en: Arpad, Azan, Elminzur, Kardam, Krum, Kurguz,
        Omurtag, Suvar, Telerig, Toktar, Unguimer, Zolta.

  Appearance
    A stunted, foul and puny people, scarcely human and
    having no language save one which bears but slight re-
    semblance to human speech. (…) Their hardihood is ev-
    ident in their wild appearance, and they are beings who
    are cruel to their children on the very day they are born.
    For they cut the cheeks of the males with a sword, so that
    before they receive the nourishment of milk they must
    learn to endure wounds. Hence they grow old beardless
    and their young men are without comeliness, because a
    face furrowed by the sword spoils by its scars the natu-
    ral beauty of a beard. They are short in stature, quick
    in bodily movement, alert horsemen, broad shouldered,
    ready in the use of bow and arrow, and have firm-set
    necks which are ever erect in pride. Though they live in
    the form of men, they have the cruelty of wild beasts.
       — Jordanes

title: Territory
leftColumn:
In short, the Huns are a “filthy race of long-haired bar-
      barians.” Indeed, they are broad-faced, quite ugly (–1 APP) and
      short (–2 SIZ), but strong and resistant (+1 STR, +1 CON),
      as Notker further notes: “The iron-like and rock-hard people
      called Huns.” These tanned and bow-legged steppe nomads,
      with rather square heads and wide chests, have long black hair
      (which the Avars wear braided) and thin mustaches. Both men
      and women wear gold earrings.
      Character
        Huns are uneducated pagan savages. The most learned
      Alcuin describes them as “a barbarian people, impervious to
      reason, uneducated, narrow-minded and slow to accept the
      holy mysteries.” They distrust buildings and are generally given
      to mysterious magical beliefs (Suspicious), they eat raw meat and
      some are said to be cannibals. They systematically rape the wom-
      en of all conquered people (Cruel, Arbitrary, Vengeful).
      Skills

        Their skills at Horsemanship and the compound Bow are
      unrivaled.
      Relations with the Franks

        In the early years, the Avars welcome the exiled Lombard
      and Bavarian enemies of Charlemagne. Later they lend their aid
      to the Slavs who try to resist the Franks. Finally, the Bulgars ally
      with Charlemagne against the Avars, who are completely defeat-
      ed (792–796). The justification for the Avar wars are, as usual,
      the sacred task to convert the pagans and steal back the liturgical
      treasures these barbarians have stolen from Christians over the
      last few centuries.
       In the palace of the Ring, the Franks discovered so much
       gold and silver and captured so much precious booty in
       their battles, that it could rightly be maintained that
       they had in all justice taken from the Huns what these
       last had unjustly stolen from other nations.
           — Einhard
        An additional motivation for Charlemagne is that he wants
      to reward those Bavarian nobles who supported him against
      Tassilo in 788, by offering them the newly conquered lands in
      the east.
       Christ, son of God, who created all peoples,
       lands, springs, rivers, mountains and formed mankind,
       has converted the Avars…
           — De Pippine Regis Victoria Avarica
        Charlemagne’s court has precious little contact with the
      other Hunnic tribes. Some missionaries are sent to convert these
      remote peoples, but with little result, despite some optimistic re-
      ports from the clergy.

    774 The Bulgar khagan Telerig discovers and executes many
      Byzantine spies.
    775 Gradasso, the noble khagan of Sericane, travels to the
      Frankish court to learn about chivalry and to win the
      sword Durendal from Roland.
    782 Avar embassy at Lippespringe. Many Avar horsemen pa-
      rade along the Bavarian frontier in order to impress the
      Franks.
    791 Khagan Kardam is victorious in war against the
      Byzantines, who pay a heavy tribute to obtain peace.
    792–796 The Franks sack the Avar Ring and finally conquer
         most of Avaria. The Tudun is baptized.
    804–806 The Bulgars conquer the remains of Avaria.
    811 The Byzantines sack Pliska, but Khagan Krum de-
      feats them while they retreat through the mountains.
      Nikephorus is killed and Krum makes a drinking cup
      from his skull.
  Territory
     The Huns rule over the plains stretching from Pannonia far
  out into Asia. Four different Hunnish lands can be distinguished:
     Avarland: The Avars live in the very isolated land that
  the ancient Romans called Pannonia, which lies between the
  Danube and the Drave. Its western border is the river Enns.
     Bulgaria: The Bulgarians live west of the Black Sea, where
  they occupy the western steppe corridor from the Dniester to
  the Danube. Their realm borders the Byzantine Empire.
     Circassia (Khazaria): On the steppe between and north of
  the Black Sea and the Caspian live the Circassians, or Khazars.
     Sericane (Mongolia): Still further east, all the way beyond
  Cathay, we find the obscure land of Sericane.
  Terrain Types

     The Huns dwell on the grass and scrubland plains known
  as the Great Steppe, where they can ride their robust ponies in
  freedom.
  Climate
     The steppe climate is characterized by very hot dry sum-
  mers and very cold winters. Similar temperature differences of-
  ten occur between day and night time.

  Travel
     Distances across the steppes are enormous. There are no
  roads, only vague trails. Huns travel along river by boats or on
  horseback through the countryside.
  Places of Interest

     The Avar Ring: The Ring is the khagan’s stronghold, a huge
  fortified camp of nine concentric earthen ramparts, where he
  keeps his treasure, situated between the Tisa and Danube Rivers.
  The commoners inside the Ring live in tents or wooden houses.

segments.text:
In short, the Huns are a “filthy race of long-haired bar-
      barians.” Indeed, they are broad-faced, quite ugly (–1 APP) and
      short (–2 SIZ), but strong and resistant (+1 STR, +1 CON),
      as Notker further notes: “The iron-like and rock-hard people
      called Huns.” These tanned and bow-legged steppe nomads,
      with rather square heads and wide chests, have long black hair
      (which the Avars wear braided) and thin mustaches. Both men
      and women wear gold earrings.
      Character
        Huns are uneducated pagan savages. The most learned
      Alcuin describes them as “a barbarian people, impervious to
      reason, uneducated, narrow-minded and slow to accept the
      holy mysteries.” They distrust buildings and are generally given
      to mysterious magical beliefs (Suspicious), they eat raw meat and
      some are said to be cannibals. They systematically rape the wom-
      en of all conquered people (Cruel, Arbitrary, Vengeful).
      Skills

Their skills at Horsemanship and the compound Bow are
      unrivaled.
      Relations with the Franks

In the early years, the Avars welcome the exiled Lombard
      and Bavarian enemies of Charlemagne. Later they lend their aid
      to the Slavs who try to resist the Franks. Finally, the Bulgars ally
      with Charlemagne against the Avars, who are completely defeat-
      ed (792–796). The justification for the Avar wars are, as usual,
      the sacred task to convert the pagans and steal back the liturgical
      treasures these barbarians have stolen from Christians over the
      last few centuries.
       In the palace of the Ring, the Franks discovered so much
       gold and silver and captured so much precious booty in
       their battles, that it could rightly be maintained that
       they had in all justice taken from the Huns what these
       last had unjustly stolen from other nations.
           — Einhard
        An additional motivation for Charlemagne is that he wants
      to reward those Bavarian nobles who supported him against
      Tassilo in 788, by offering them the newly conquered lands in
      the east.
       Christ, son of God, who created all peoples,
       lands, springs, rivers, mountains and formed mankind,
       has converted the Avars…
           — De Pippine Regis Victoria Avarica
        Charlemagne’s court has precious little contact with the
      other Hunnic tribes. Some missionaries are sent to convert these
      remote peoples, but with little result, despite some optimistic re-
      ports from the clergy.

title: Society
leftColumn:
The land of the Avars used to be encircled by nine rings.
       Every ring was built of logs of oak, beech and fir. It was
       twenty feet wide from edge to edge, and it was the same
       height. All the space inside was filled with hard stone
       and heavy clay. Small trees were planted within the
       ring, and when these were lopped and trained to bend
       forwards, they presented an impenetrable screen of twigs
       and foliage. Between these ramparts lied hamlets and
       farmsteads. From the second ring, which was built ex-
       actly like the first, to the third one, stretched some twenty
       miles. So it continued to the ninth, although, of course,
       each consecutive ring was considerably smaller than the
       previous one.
           — Notker
        Cherson: The capital of Circassia on the Crimean
      Peninsula.
        Pliska: The Bulgar capital is a large town surrounded by
      a moat and earthwork ramparts containing the palace and reli-
      gious buildings. The inner fortress has walls 12 meters high built
      of limestone blocks held together with mortar. The royal area
      has paved streets and an ingenious sewer system.
      Society
        Hunnic nobles are horse-riding nomads, moving around in
      yurt camps to exert their power over large territories. They live
      in symbiosis with the settled agrarian population, often subdued
      Slav peasants from whom they extort tributes. As a people, the
      Huns are often disorganized, divided by internal strife and quar-
      rels of succession. Their chiefs are named khagan (king), tudun
      (duke) and tarkan (count). Queens bear the title of katun.
        The position of khagan is sometimes purely a sacred or cer-
      emonial one, with the real political and military power being
      wielded by a tudun, who then takes the title of khagan-bäg. This
      is notably the case in Avarland.
        The Avar submission lasts from 791 to 805. During this
      period, many Avars flee to the neighboring Bulgar kingdom of
      Khagan Krum (803–814). The Avars are reduced to the same
      level as the local Slavs they formerly dominated, and over the
      years they become a single people with them.
      Religion
        Apart from the Khazars (Circassians), Huns are pagans
      who worship a pantheon of nature gods, of whom Tangra is the
      leader. Their rituals center around ancestors and spirits. The
      burial rites for nobles consist of cremation, together with their
      gold, weapons, horses and slaves.
        In the last Paladin phase, the Avars are Christianized from
      Salzburg, but even before that period missionaries are sent out to
      convert the Huns. They actually make some Christian converts
      among the nobles. Note that Jewish and Persian missionaries are
      also active among the Hunnish pagans.
        Surprisingly, the Circassians are Jews, but without the
      Talmudic theology.
rightColumn:
At the present time we know of no nation under the heav-
    ens where Christians do not live. For Christians are even
    found in the lands of Gog and Magog — who are a Hun-
    nic race and are called Khazars. They are circumcised
    and observing the laws of Judaism. The Bulgars, howev-
    er, who are of the same seven tribes as the Khazars, are
    now becoming baptized into Christianity.
       — Abbot Christian of Stavelot-Malmédy
  Daily Life and Economy
     The common Huns are semi-nomadic pastoralists keeping
  herds of cattle, goats, sheep and horses. Given the immense ter-
  ritory on which they live, population density is unsurprisingly
  low.
     Rich noble Hunnish men have many women, but adultery
  is severely punished: adulterers are quartered by horses or bent
  trees. When a khagan dies, he usually leaves many children from
  different women, which causes a period of political instability
  until a new khagan takes power.
     The Huns are often wealthy, but have few commercial rela-
  tions with the outside world. They even block the trade on the
  Danube. “At that time, the Avars, the Bulgars and many other sav-
  age races barred the overland route to Byzantium,” — Notker.
  They use smoke signals to communicate over great distances.
     The only artisanal skill of which the Huns have a great mas-
  tery is metal working (silver, gold, and bronze). They invented
  the stirrup.
  Warfare

     Young Hunnish warriors must prove themselves by bring-
  ing back the head or nose of their first human kill. Once accept-
  ed as men, they are given their own pony and may participate in
  military expeditions.
     The Bulgars are continually at war with Byzantium, while
  the Avars exercise a reign of terror in central Europe. They reg-
  ularly conduct very fast raids into Lombardy or Bavaria, where
  they pillage churches and collect “peace tributes.” On horseback
  they are able to cover enormous distances at great speed. They
  prefer swooping cavalry raids, aided by bow fire from horseback,
  and often use Slavs as human shields when retreating. Note that
  rain sometimes hampers their archery. While raiding, they aim
  at collecting riches and taking women for slaves.
     While they are masters of the art of mobile warfare, their
  tactics lose a lot of efficiency in a pitched defensive battle.
  Standard Equipment
     Nobles: Cuirbouilli and open helmet (7 points), light
  shield (3 points); scimitar, compound bow, dagger; steppe pony
  with felt (2 points) or lamellar (4 points) horse-armor.
     Mounted archers: Fur clothes and cap (5 points), light
  shield (3 points); compound bow, dagger; steppe pony with felt
  (2 points) or lamellar (4 points) horse-armor.

title: Society
leftColumn:
Footmen: Furs (5 points) and light shield (3 points); jave-
      lin, compound bow, dagger.
      Code of Honor
        The Huns follow their leader as long as he is successful in
      war. They do not follow the codes of knighthood or chivalry,
      and their word cannot be trusted.

      Fortifications
        Having little or no siege equipment and very little skill
      in siege-craft and other forms of immobile warfare, they rare-
      ly attack or defend fortifications. In the open field, they set up
      their wagons in a circular camp. All in all, defense is a Hunnic
      weakness.
      Jews

      Names
      M
           en: Aaron, Abraham, Benjamin, Daniel, David,
           Eleazar, Eliah, Isaac, Joseph, Nathan, Ruben,
           Salomon, Samuel, Sedechias, Simon.
        Women: Deborah, Esther, Hannah, Lydia, Miriam, Naomi,
      Rachel, Rebecca.
        Many Frankish Jews latinize their names, so Nathan be-
      comes Donatus and Isaac calls himself Gaudiocus. Some assimi-
      lated Jews simply give their children Frankish names.
      Appearance
        Jews are slightly smaller (–1 SIZ) and often much less mus-
      cular then Franks (–2 STR). They have an aquiline profile and
      usually dress in robes.
      Character

        Jews are generally known as hard workers (Energetic,
      Modest, and Temperate). Their shrewd merchants have a rep-
      utation of being Honest and Prudent, but quite Selfish at times.
      Skills
        Jews are praised as trustworthy merchants (Stewardship)
      who travel everywhere in Europe and beyond. They are always
      literate and often speak many tongues (Reading & Writing,

Let no Jew presume to have a money-changer’s table in
       his house, nor shall he presume to sell wine, grain, or
       other commodities there. But if it be discovered that he
       has done so all his goods shall be taken away from him,
       and he shall be imprisoned until he is brought into our
       presence.
           — Capitulary for the Jews
      Warfare

        The Jews have no army. They are exempt from military
      service, since Charlemagne’s army is explicitly a Christian one.
      They are not allowed to carry weapons. For their protection,
      Jewish merchants are often accompanied by Gascon, Visigoth or
      Lombard mercenary knights.

        The name “Longobards”/”Lombards” means “long-beards.”
      The Lombards wear short mantles, wide trousers and leather
      boots. They have beards and grow their hair long, but shave the
      back of the head. Women wear Roman-style dresses and jewelry.

       All a Lombard wants is to fill his stomach with wine and
        his house with gold.
           — Frankish saying

        The Pope describes the decadent Lombards in a letter to
      Charlemagne and Carloman, in which he asks both Frankish
      kings not to marry a Lombard princess, for “the faithless and
      most vile Lombards (…) have certainly brought forth the lep-
      ers.” While not all Lombards are vile and untrustworthy, most
      of them have certain character flaws such as Deceitful, Lustful,
      Lazy, Indulgent, Proud, Selfish and Cowardly.

      do they become more appreciated for their emulation of the
      dominant Carolingian culture. They are not particularly not-
      ed for their courage or energy, but most Lombards are fervent
      Christians (Love [God]).

  Relations with the Franks

     At first, the Lombards are allied to the Franks by three roy-
  al weddings: Tassilo of Bavaria, Carloman and Charlemagne
  each marry a daughter of the Lombard king. However, when
  Charlemagne repudiates his wife and Carloman dies in 771,
  things change radically. Two years later, when King Desiderius
  threatens to take Rome, Charlemagne invades and conquers
  Lombardy. Once the Lombards become part of the Frankish
  empire, many become loyal vassals of Charlemagne. Those who
  resist the Frankish king flee to Benevento, Spoleto, Byzantium,
  Bavaria or Avarland. The Byzantines become allies in their re-
  volt against the Franks in Italy.
  Chronology
    767 A Lombard-Frankish alliance defeats the Saracens who
      besiege Rome.
    768 King Desiderius mutilates councilors of the new Pope.
    770 Charlemagne marries Princess Desideria of Pavia.
    771 Charlemagne repudiates Queen Desideria. King
      Carloman dies and his widow, Princess Gerberga, flees
      to Pavia.
    772 King Desiderius marches to Rome with an army. The
      Pope calls on Charlemagne for help.
    773 Charlemagne invades Lombardy.
    774 Charlemagne is crowned King of the Lombards.
    775 Secret alliance between several exiled Lombard dukes.
    776 Charlemagne crushes a revolt in Friuli.
    777 After a failed revolt, Duke Arichis of Benevento pledges
      fealty to Charlemagne.

      gaged to Prince Constantine VI of Byzantium.
    787 Charlemagne restores the order in Benevento and in-
      stalls Grimoald as the new duke.

leftColumn:
found inland, while gulfs and bays pierce the rocky coast. The
      smoking pinnacle of Mount Vesuvius can be seen for miles.
        The Italian climate has hot dry summers and relatively mild
      winters, apart from in the northern Po valley and in the moun-
      tain areas, where temperatures may drop significantly during
      winter.
        To reach Italy by land, there are only two safe passes through
      the Alps: the Saint Bernard Pass and the Brenner Pass. Some
      other minor passes exist, but they are extremely dangerous. Most
      common travelers use the Roman roads, which are still in a rea-
      sonable state. In northern Lombardy, much transport goes via
      the Po River. Important sea harbors exist over the entire coastal
      area, facilitating maritime trade with Byzantium and Arabia.
      Places of Interest
        Aosta: A fortified Roman mountain town that guards the
      Saint Bernard Pass across the Alps to Burgundy.
        Assisi: This cathedral town is completely destroyed in 773,
      but later restored with the great castle of Rocca d’Assisi.
        Benevento: The capital of the Beneventan duchy is situat-
      ed on a hill, with a thriving market and a cathedral. It has pre-
      served the strong Roman city walls and a bath house.
        Bobbio: This rich abbey under royal protection is famous
      for the tomb of Saint Colombanus and its scriptorium. Umberto
      is the abbot here.
        Bologna: The town has the first and only Italian universi-
      ty, located within the city walls. The gastald lives in a very high
      wooden tower with a stone first floor.
        Brindisi: An important Beneventan town in the “heel” of
      Italy with a fortified harbor bay.

San Vicenzo al Volturno: This abbey is famous for its
  well-maintained scriptorium.
     Spoleto: A wealthy and independent town on top of a hill
  with city walls, a medium wooden castle and an amphitheater.
     Venice: An important an independent merchant city in
  the saltwater lagoon of the Po River. Venice is the capital of a
  Byzantine exarchate. It has a fortified harbor.
     Verona: An important walled city along the Po River,
  which serves as the residence of the Lombard princes. Within
  the city walls are a stone stronghold, a monastery, a basilica and
  a Roman arena. The city has been described eloquently by an
  anonymous Carolingian poet:
    It forms a square, its walls are strongly built,
    Forty-eight towers in a circuit brilliantly gleam,
    And eight lofty ones among them are taller than all the
     others.
    It has a high labyrinth in the shape of a great ring
    From which he who enters unknowingly cannot escape,
    Except by the light of a lantern or with a ball of thread.

    It has a wide and spacious forum paved with stones,
    At each of its four angles stands a great arch,
    And its streets are wondrously laid with flagstones.
    A lofty citadel provides a strong bastion against attack,
    There are stone bridges built over the wide river,
    The heads of which link the town and the citadel.

  Society

     The Lombard king resides permanently in his magnificent
  court at Pavia. He is allied with the Bavarians and Byzantium.
     Lombard cities are governed by urban counts named gast-
  alds. They generally seek to reinforce their own autonomy and
  regularly challenge the central authority of their sovereign. The
  king has little real power, for he depends on his great vassals. The
  problem is that they care more for their own interests, and tend
  to furnish few troops for the royal army. The real seats of power
  are the wealthy fortified cities, leaving the countryside almost
  entirely without defense.
  Religion
     The Lombards are Christians. Some of the largest and most
  famous monasteries and abbeys thrive in Lombardy.
  Daily Life

     The Italian peninsula is quite urbanized compared to the
  rest of the realm, much like Romanized lands such as Septimania
  and Provence. The rich Italian cities are walled and often have
  paved streets, bath houses, and various other Roman monu-
  ments like great statues, an aqueduct, or an amphitheater.
