title: Warfare
leftColumn:
Economy
        Wealth is primarily based on the important urban produc-
      tion centers and on long distance trade. Cities like Pavia and
      Venice are counted among the great ports for Oriental products.

      Warfare
        Lombards are rich and well-equipped. Like the Franks,
      they fight predominantly with shock cavalry. Urban militias
      fight only to defend their city and never follow their gastald on
      campaign abroad.

      Standard Equipment
        Nobles: Scale armor (12 points), shield (6 points); spear,
      sword, dagger; charger and rouncy (like the Romans, Lombard
      knights wear a cross on their helmet).
        Footmen/Urban militia: Cuirbouilli (6 points), shield (6
      points); spear, hand axe, bow, dagger.
      Code of Honor

        The Lombards have a peculiar con-
      cept of honor and knighthood. Nobles
      derive a significant part of their author-
      ity from their wealth and mercantile
      success. Much like
rightColumn:
the Saracens, the world of the Lombards is all about money.
  In short, Lombard lords care more about the economic health
  of their city than for battle prowess and glory. Still, Lombard
  knights value their public credibility and a given word is sacred.
  Fortifications
     Lombard lords do not build their castles in the country, but
  exclusively inside their cities. Such a castle is usually integrated
  into the city walls and other defensive works. However, the king
  can order the construction of a fortress in the general interest of
  the Lombard people, such as the Lombard Narrows.

  Moors    and  Saracens

  T
      he Moors and Saracens are related, in that the Moors are
      Saracens who conquered and settled in Spain. Saracens
      can be found across the entire north coast of Africa, from
  Arabia in the east, to the Strait of Gibraltar in the west.
  Names
     Men: Abilant, Acars, Aelroth, Aerofle, Agrapars, Almari,
  Alphaien, Amandras, Amargon, Amborre, Blancandrin,
  Boidant, Burdel, Calides, Canabeus, Chernubles, Clarien,
  Clarifan, Climborin, Corsalis, Corsolt, Dapamort, Eliades,
  Escababi, Escremiz, Esperrant, Esperveres, Estamarin,
  Estorgans, Estramariz, Esturguz, Estropin, Faldrun, Falsaron,
  Floriades, Galafres, Galindres, Gamalfin, Grandonie, Grishart,
  Grossaille, Guarlan, Haucebier, Jangleu, Juner, Jurfaleu,
  Lanpal, Machiner, Maladient, Malbien, Malcuid, Malpalin,
  Malpramis, Malquiant, Maltraien, Malun, Mandaquin,
  Marcule, Margariz, Moadas, Moysant, Pantalis, Priamon,
  Rodoan, Salatiel, Siglorel, Sinagon, Thiorin, Timozel, Torleu,
  Triamodes, Turgis, Uliens, Valdabrun, Walegrape, Yvorin.
     Women: Bramimunda, Floripas, Galacienne, Orable.
  Appearance
     Most have curly black hair and copper, brown or black
  skin. Men wear short pointy beards and sometimes a thin mus-
  tache. However, the Saracens from the North African moun-
  tains are often fair-haired and blue-eyed. They are not the
  most resilient of all people (–1 SIZ), but have a certain natural
  agility (+1 DEX).
     Like the Persians, Saracen men wear turbans. Ladies often
  wear large round golden earrings. Unmarried women hide their
  nose and mouth behind a transparent veil.
  Character
     As pagans their characters are necessarily flawed. Their
  vices are numerous: they are cunning liars and regularly betray
  others and themselves (Deceitful, Arbitrary), they are extremely
  boastful (Proud), they sometimes torture their prisoners or sell
  them as slaves (Cruel).

title: Relations with the Franks
leftColumn:
The emir has commanded a raiding gang all night!
       He’s taken towns and country-keeps alike;
       He’s hacked the head of many a lawful squire
       And slit the breasts of their defenseless wives;
       He’s given their girls, all daughters of fine knights

        (…) to the scum at his side,
       Then bound them all in chains, criminal-like;
       These girls cry out, lamenting loud their plight:
       “O, Charlemagne! Come and avenge this crime!”
       For gold and coin they’re bought and sold meanwhile.
           — Song of Aspremont, III

        To boost their relatively low valor (Cowardly), some
      Saracens drink the blood of tigers, antelopes, and giraffes.They
      have a comparatively low Love [family]:
       “Tell Charlemagne you will follow him to Aachen
       And receive the Christian faith;
       You will be his vassal in honor and in all your goods.
       If he asks you hostages, send him some,
       Either ten or twenty, as a mark of good faith.

       Let us send him the sons of our wives;
       Even if it means his death, I shall send him mine.
       Far better for them to lose their heads there
       Than for us to lose our honor and our lands
       And be reduced to begging.”
           — Song of Roland, III

        On the other hand, their culture highly values moderation
      in sexual and other appetites (Chaste, Temperate).
      Skills
        The pagan science of healing is largely superior to the ru-
      dimentary skills of the Frankish monks (First Aid, Chirurgery).
      The Saracens have a long tradition of horsemanship and trick
      riding (Horsemanship). Their mercantile society gives them sig-
      nificant skill in Stewardship.
      Relations with the Franks

        At first, the Saracen attitude toward the Franks varies from
      awe and admiration to open hostility. To distinguish themselves
      from the merchants, feudalized Moorish nobles try to uphold
      the ideals of honor and knighthood, which creates a sort of
      solidarity with Frankish knights. Therefore, Frankish exiles are
      often warmly welcomed by their noble counterparts at Saracen
      courts. In his youth, Charlemagne himself served the Moorish
      emir as an exiled mercenary knight!
        As the Paladin chronology advances, the initial respect
      fades and cedes its place to mutual hatred. After the Battle of
      Roncevaux many Christians from Spain seek refuge north of the
rightColumn:
Pyrenees. In the Frankish mind, the Mozarabs (Arab-speaking
  Christians living in Spain, a majority of the population!) are se-
  verely oppressed. One of the unexpected results for the Saracens
  is a sort of tacit alliance with the Byzantines in mutual opposi-
  tion to the Franks and Persians.
  Chronology
    754 King Pepin captures the city of Narbonne.
    759 King Pepin liberates Septimania.
    765 Marsile is crowned emir.

    767 The Franks liberate Rome from the Saracens at the
      Battle of the Humble Squires.
    769 The Saracens are defeated at the siege of Milan.
    771 Charlemagne leads his troops across the Pyrenees and
      sacks several towns.
    776 The siege of Biserta is resolved by a threefold duel with
      the Franks. Agramant, Sobrino and Gradasso are killed.
    777 The Wali of Barcelona asks Charlemagne to help him
      liberate Spain from Emir Marsile’s oppression.
    778 Emir Marsile and Sultan Baligant are defeated at the
      battle of Roncevaux.
    779 The Moors are forced to recognize Anseïs of Carthago
      as the first Frankish Duke of Spain. Marsile breaks the
      peace treaty and is decapitated for treason.
    780 Hisham succeeds his father Marsile as emir of Cordoba.
      The giant Sultan of Babylon, Bruhier, raids Frankland,
      but he is defeated by Ogier the Dane.
    781 William Shortnose slays the Saracen giant Corsolt in a
      duel near Rome.
    782 Internecine wars in the Sultanate of Babylon.
    788 Emir Hisham declares a holy war against the Franks and
      raids Septimania.
    790 William Shortnose liberates Nîmes from the Moors.
    791 Orange is taken by William Shortnose.
    792 The Franks liberate Vivien, held captive at Luiserna.
    793 Battle of the Archant, where Vivien dies.
    794 Rainouart defeats Gadifer in a duel.
    797 Many nobles accused of treason are decapitated (“Day
      of the Ditch”).

title: Territory and Nations
leftColumn:
Territory and Nations

        Emirate of Cordoba: The Saracens of the Iberian
      Peninsula, or Moors, conquered the Gothic Kingdom in 711. It
      is now divided into 4 regions: Baetica in the south (Cordoba),
      Lusitania in the south-west (Luiserna), Carthago in the cen-
      ter (Toledo), and Tarraconensis in the north-east (Barcelona),
      which the Franks call Gothland or the Spanish March (once it
      comes under Frankish rule).
        Sultanate of Babylon: The Saracen empire covers a vast
      territory from Arabia to Barbary (Northern Africa), including
      the legendary cities of Babylon (Cairo) and Alexandria.
      Terrain Types and Climate
        Emirate of Cordoba: The southern Iberian Peninsula is a
      dry, hot region with many olive trees. The north is mostly cov-
      ered with temperate grasslands and foothills, which are separat-
      ed from Frankland by the steep Pyrenees Mountains.
        Sultanate of Babylon: The Northern African coast con-
      sists of a small strip of cultivated hills and plains. The Nile
      valley is very fertile, especially its delta at the shores of the
      Mediterranean. A mountain range separates the northern coast
      from the African interior, which is mostly hot rocky and sandy
      deserts. On the eastern coast of the Red Sea lies Arabia, which
      has rocky hills in the east and an endless sandy desert stretching
      out east and north all the way up to Persia.
        The African and Arabian climate has dry hot summers with
      strong dusty winds or even dust storms. Water is scarce every-
      where, but in the rainy season flash floods are frequent.
      Travel
        Emirate of Cordoba: Like in the rest of western Europe,
      ancient Roman roads survive in Spain. Though most have
      fallen into disrepair, they are still used by travelers, merchants
      and armies. Across the vast stretches of uncharted land, where
      no such roads exist, sheep paths offer a viable alternative route
      for travelers. All in all, these conditions do not favor the use of
      wheeled vehicles. Saracen knights largely prefer camels or horses,
      while merchants ride donkeys or pack mules. In the north, the
      Ebro river is navigable almost the entire way up to the Pyrenees.
        Sultanate of Babylon: The easiest way for Franks to go to
      Africa or Arabia is by ship. Saracen or Jewish merchants assure
      regular connections to the important cities of the Mediterranean
      basin. Ships sail in convoys, setting out in spring and returning
      after summer.
        In Africa, the caravan roads in the coastal regions are easi-
      ly traveled, but to cross the desert camels are to be preferred to
      horses, and one needs to have a guide who knows where the wa-
      dis and the oasis are.
rightColumn:
Places of Interest

  eMirate of cordoba
     Andrenas [Alicante]: A small stone castle high on the
  rocks dominates this walled harbor town. The coastline consists
  of saltwater wetlands, but the hinterland are arid rocky hills cov-
  ered with shrubs.
     Barbastro: A relatively independent town with a stone
  border castle in the southern Pyrenees, to the north-west of
  Barcelona. Its siege (802) is one of the most bloody episodes of
  the Spanish conquest.
     Barcelona: A town with exceptionally strong Roman city
  walls. Inside the city stands the Idol With The Key:
    On the shore of the sea is an old hollow stone, finely
    carved, of Saracen workmanship, set on the ground. It
    was wide and four-sided below, and narrower and nar-
    rower above, as high as the flight of a crow in the air.
    And on that stone is an image made of the finest brass,
    in the fashion of a man standing on his feet, with his face
    towards the south, and in his right hand a huge key.
       — Welsh Pseudo-Turpin (Llyfr Coch Hergest)
     Candie [Gandia/Valencia]: A fortified trading town with
  a wide network of irrigation canals, which allow agriculture to
  flourish.
     Cordoba: The immense and very wealthy Moorish capital
  on the Guadalquivir River is protected by a double wall with
  50 towers and a powerful citadel, called Morinda. It has seven
  bridges, and as many permanent markets, where merchants from
  all over the world come to do their business.
     Lerida: A small inland town protected by a tall stone tow-
  er, the home of Wali Zuda.
     Majorca: Aigremor is the capital of the rather independent
  island, governed by the courteous Wali Ganor. A large, impen-
  etrable prison tower called Aufalerne stands high upon a rocky
  hill.
     Monbranc [Medinaceli]: This stronghold is situated in a
  mountain pass and defends the Moorish border with Asturias. It
  is held by a line of independent walis.
     Loquiferne [Castellón de la Plana, Fadrell Castle]: At
  the center of this walled harbor town stands a high stone tower.
  Rainouart was born here.
     Luiserna [Lisbon]: A tolerant and independent Visigothic
  wali holds this fortified harbor town, which specializes in the
  trade of slaves, wine, salt and horses.
     Portpaillart [Montgri Castle, Gerona]: A harbor town
  defended by the impregnable Tower of Ayete, which serves as
  Tiebaut’s treasure chamber.

title: Society
leftColumn:
Saragossa: The biggest pagan-held city of northern Spain.
      Its largely Visigothic population is often hostile to the emir, but
      not much more favorable to the Franks. The local wali lives in a
      stone fortress called Aljaferia.
        Toledo: The great Roman city of Toledo has a famous uni-
      versity, and the largest permanent slave market of Spain.
        Tortosa: Surrounded by rocky hills, the fortified harbor of
      Tortosa is strategically built on the southern bank of the Ebro
      River, where it is defended by a stone castle.
      sultaNate of babyloN
        Alexandria: This city in the Nile delta is a center of the
      cloth and spice trade with Persia and beyond. Its city walls are
      protected by 140 stone towers. In its center stands the immense
      marble lighthouse, which is permanently lit by a magical carbun-
      cle. This so-called Tower of Maidens contains the sultan’s harem.
      It has three levels; a central pillar contains the stairs and the ad-
      jacent royal lodging are connected to the tower’s second floor by
      a suspended gallery. The tower is guarded day and night by 14
      eunuchs, and it is forbidden even to look at the tower gate. The
      tower and the sultan’s palace are surrounded by the Nile and the
      magnificent palace gardens, which contain the Source of Purity.
      Only virgins can touch its water without staining it. In the gar-
      dens grows a Tree of Love, which has eternal red flowers.
        Algiers: A walled town of Roman origin on the Northern
      African coast, with a fortified harbor and a stone castle.
        Babylon [Cairo]: The magnificent Arab capital is famous
      for the Palace of the Sultan, which can be accessed via a bridge
      with four successive gate towers. It is surrounded by magnificent
      gardens watered by a magic source of youthfulness, which is
      guarded by a serpent. The palace roofs are covered with hanging
      gardens, irrigated by means of water-wheels.
        Biserta [Tunis]: A large fortress in northern Africa with a
      strong citadel and fortified harbor. The city is renowned for its
      mules and silks.
        Kairouan: A stronghold in the middle of a forest with
      many wild animals, which has grown into a prosperous market
      town with lush gardens. It was initially built to protect the trade
      road from Babylon to Cordoba from the aggressive desert tribes.
      Society
        In theory, the Saracens live in a feudal society. Normally,
      feudalism is based on a fief and an oath of fealty. The Saracen
      emirs not only grant land or titles, but also the control of rivers
      (vital for water supplies). However, these benefices are often not
      linked to vassalage, and vassalage does not require the grant of a
      fief. These land gifts are more like temporary presents to reward
      loyal followers or appease rivals. So, even though the concepts of
      knighthood and chivalry (and later even Romance as well) have
      found their way to Saracen society, there is no tightly-structured
      feudal hierarchy.
        Saracen culture is deeply suffused with ancient tribal re-
      lations, where empty titles and the prestige of lineage is more
rightColumn:
important than land ownership and military prowess. The
  delicate power balance between the great families depends on
  temporary alliances. Tribes or military confederations live in
  geographical isolation from one another and sometimes have
  opposing interests. Internecine wars and rebellions are frequent,
  so the emir must rule with both delicacy and firmness.
     In reality, money is what really holds Saracen society to-
  gether. Gold and silk are all that count for the rich middle class
  of artisans and merchants. Their non-feudal commercial inter-
  ests often effectively harness the wali’s tribal interests and his
  military ambitions.
     Justice is concentrated in the towns. Indeed, as a ruling mi-
  nority in Spain, the Moors have established their power base in-
  side fortified cities, leaving the direct control of the countryside
  to local rulers, often Mozarabs. These rural lords have a certain
  autonomy, as long as they pay tribute to the wali. In all Saracen
  towns, the wali has the right to demand the inhabitants to spend
  a specified time working on road or bridge maintenance.
     The primary Saracen weakness is their internal division,
  even to the point where the emir calls on Christians or Jews for
  delicate and confidential tasks. Such persons are often promoted
  to high administrative offices. The death of an emir or sultan in-
  variably gives rise to internal strife and a ferocious power struggle
  between influential families.

Saragossa: The biggest pagan-held city of northern Spain.
      Its largely Visigothic population is often hostile to the emir, but
      not much more favorable to the Franks. The local wali lives in a
      stone fortress called Aljaferia.
        Toledo: The great Roman city of Toledo has a famous uni-
      versity, and the largest permanent slave market of Spain.
        Tortosa: Surrounded by rocky hills, the fortified harbor of
      Tortosa is strategically built on the southern bank of the Ebro
      River, where it is defended by a stone castle.
      sultaNate of babyloN
        Alexandria: This city in the Nile delta is a center of the
      cloth and spice trade with Persia and beyond. Its city walls are
      protected by 140 stone towers. In its center stands the immense
      marble lighthouse, which is permanently lit by a magical carbun-
      cle. This so-called Tower of Maidens contains the sultan’s harem.
      It has three levels; a central pillar contains the stairs and the ad-
      jacent royal lodging are connected to the tower’s second floor by
      a suspended gallery. The tower is guarded day and night by 14
      eunuchs, and it is forbidden even to look at the tower gate. The
      tower and the sultan’s palace are surrounded by the Nile and the
      magnificent palace gardens, which contain the Source of Purity.
      Only virgins can touch its water without staining it. In the gar-
      dens grows a Tree of Love, which has eternal red flowers.
        Algiers: A walled town of Roman origin on the Northern
      African coast, with a fortified harbor and a stone castle.
        Babylon [Cairo]: The magnificent Arab capital is famous
      for the Palace of the Sultan, which can be accessed via a bridge
      with four successive gate towers. It is surrounded by magnificent
      gardens watered by a magic source of youthfulness, which is
      guarded by a serpent. The palace roofs are covered with hanging
      gardens, irrigated by means of water-wheels.
        Biserta [Tunis]: A large fortress in northern Africa with a
      strong citadel and fortified harbor. The city is renowned for its
      mules and silks.
        Kairouan: A stronghold in the middle of a forest with
      many wild animals, which has grown into a prosperous market
      town with lush gardens. It was initially built to protect the trade
      road from Babylon to Cordoba from the aggressive desert tribes.
      Society
        In theory, the Saracens live in a feudal society. Normally,
      feudalism is based on a fief and an oath of fealty. The Saracen
      emirs not only grant land or titles, but also the control of rivers
      (vital for water supplies). However, these benefices are often not
      linked to vassalage, and vassalage does not require the grant of a
      fief. These land gifts are more like temporary presents to reward
      loyal followers or appease rivals. So, even though the concepts of
      knighthood and chivalry (and later even Romance as well) have
      found their way to Saracen society, there is no tightly-structured
      feudal hierarchy.
        Saracen culture is deeply suffused with ancient tribal re-
      lations, where empty titles and the prestige of lineage is more

important than land ownership and military prowess. The
  delicate power balance between the great families depends on
  temporary alliances. Tribes or military confederations live in
  geographical isolation from one another and sometimes have
  opposing interests. Internecine wars and rebellions are frequent,
  so the emir must rule with both delicacy and firmness.
     In reality, money is what really holds Saracen society to-
  gether. Gold and silk are all that count for the rich middle class
  of artisans and merchants. Their non-feudal commercial inter-
  ests often effectively harness the wali’s tribal interests and his
  military ambitions.
     Justice is concentrated in the towns. Indeed, as a ruling mi-
  nority in Spain, the Moors have established their power base in-
  side fortified cities, leaving the direct control of the countryside
  to local rulers, often Mozarabs. These rural lords have a certain
  autonomy, as long as they pay tribute to the wali. In all Saracen
  towns, the wali has the right to demand the inhabitants to spend
  a specified time working on road or bridge maintenance.
     The primary Saracen weakness is their internal division,
  even to the point where the emir calls on Christians or Jews for
  delicate and confidential tasks. Such persons are often promoted
  to high administrative offices. The death of an emir or sultan in-
  variably gives rise to internal strife and a ferocious power struggle
  between influential families.

  walis act as more or less independent rulers, and these urban
  magnates themselves are confronted with rural lords claiming
  autonomy. Feudalism is only loosely established and the emir
  wields little power outside the main cities. The walis are often
  tempted to assert their independence from Cordoba and look to
  the Franks for support, though the last thing they want is to live
  under Frankish dominion.

  half of the 8th century, the frontier region between the emirate
  and the Visigothic kingdom of Asturias has been almost devoid

  and small castles. Boars, bears and wolves roam unmolested in
  these uninhabited, often sterile, buffer territories.

  gods as statues on the battlefield.

    Their great mouths leer like evil things begot;

title: Warfare
leftColumn:
However, their faith is not very strong, and whenever a sit-
      uation is not to their liking the Saracens blame their powerless
      gods in a violent manner:
       The Saracens rush off to Apollo in a crypt,
       Rail against him and hurl abuse at him:
       “O, wretched god, why do you cause us such shame?
       Why did you permit our king to be destroyed?
       Anyone who serves you well receives a poor reward.”

       Then they grab his scepter and his crown
       And hang him from his hands from a pillar;
       Then they send him flying to the ground at their feet
       And beat him and smash him to pieces with sticks.
       They seize Tervagant’s carbuncle
       And fling Muhammad into a ditch

       Where pigs and dogs bite and trample on him.
           — Song of Roland, CLXXXVII
        The Mozarabs are the Arabic-speaking, Visigothic Christian
      population of Moorish Spain. To practice their religion, Christians
      and Jews must pay the dhimmi, an annual poll-tax. This protects
      them from persecution and even gives them certain rights, but
      excludes them from holding political power inside the cities.
      Christians and Jews have their own churches and courts.
        The Christian churches on the Spanish peninsula hold
      many saints’ and martyrs’ relics, which attract emissaries from
      Frankish bishops and abbots who wish to buy (or steal) them.
      Daily Life and Economy
        A small number of Saracens are nomadic desert folk who ride
      on camels and live in tents. However, most Saracens live in cities.
      Houses are usually built from tamped earth. Since water is a con-
      stant problem, all cities are situated in river valleys. The surround-
      ing fields are irrigated either by chain wells (a series of linked un-
      derground wells), or by norias (waterwheels with buckets driven
      by donkeys in order to lift underground water to the field).
        The numerous, often very large, cities have very narrow and sin-
      uous streets, and in their central market squares a temple can usually
      be found. A Master of the Market (sahib al-suq) controls this central
      area, which is strictly non-residential and deserted at night, when it is
      patrolled by guards. Jews usually have their own walled quarter. The
      wali lives in his citadel castle (alcazar) along the city wall.
        Saracen society has given rise to burgeoning urban-craft in-
      dustries. Even during times of war, many caravans travel along
      the main trade routes, though political instability does not fa-
      vor the commercial routes from Frankland leading into Spain
      via Saragossa. Saracen merchants trade with all other cultures
      around the Mediterranean Sea. Indeed, trade is so important
      in the Saracen world that their entire empire is a free trade area
      where one’s origin is no bar to travel. Foreign merchants are
      treated with respect, for commercial interests outweigh military
      hostility. Like the Byzantines and Persians, Saracen merchants
      prefer gold coins or silk bundles to silver pieces.
rightColumn:
Saracens are especially known for their flourishing slave
  trade. Note that no Moorish or Saracen slaves are allowed, nor
  can law-abiding tax-paying foreigners be enslaved. Slaves in
  Spain tend to be employed as domestic servants, administrators
  and soldiers, rather than peasants obliged to work in the fields.
     Moorish cities are famous for their leather, camels and pure-
  bred horses. Though well supplied with most luxury goods (silks,
  perfume, glass), the Moors have a chronic need for wood, since
  their lands are not very forested. The rural population, mostly
  Visigothic, make their living from sheep herding and farming ce-
  real crops, grapevines and olive trees. Like the Persians, the Moors
  and Saracens practice intensive hydraulic agriculture around their
  cities. Inside the towns and cities lofty gardens produce fruits.
  Warfare
     The Saracens have a permanent standing army composed
  of askaris (warriors) and foreign mercenary soldiers. The better
  equipped nobles are faris, the equivalent of the Frankish knights.
  An almansour is a sort of banneret, while a wali is the ruler over a
  town or a small district (a kura, plural kuwar), quite like a count.
  A king is called an emir. The highest rank is that of sultan, com-
  parable to an emperor. Saracens sometimes count enslaved giants
  or centaurs among their ranks. The Moors carry a white stan-
  dard, the Sultan of Babylon raises a green banner.
     While they sometimes engage in full scale battles with the
  Franks, the Saracens are more feared for their quick raids and
  their piracy on the Mediterranean Sea. Their goal is often not
  conquest but the capture of plunder and slaves.
  Standard Equipment
     Faris: Light chain mail and a pointy helmet (10 points),
  small round shield (4 points); scimitar, mace, lance, compound
  bow, curved dagger; courser, charger, or camel.
     Askaris: Cuirbouilli and a pointy helmet (6 points), small
  round shield (4 points); spear, compound bow, curved dagger;
  courser.
     Footmen: Soft leather (4 points), small round shield (4
  points); spear, mace, bow, curved dagger.

  Code of Honor
     The Moors and Saracens recognize some chivalric customs,
  like judicial combat to resolve conflicts. To them, such a trial by
  combat duel is a cynical challenge to the Christian God to prove
  His power.
    “For the city which is my inherited right
    choose any man who is valiant in fight
    and I shall choose one of my line.
    Then we shall of our champions make trial.

    If your God has the power to inspire
    the defeat of my champion by your knight,
    then you will hold Rome free and for life.”
       — The Coronation of Louis, XVIII

title: Relations with the Franks
leftColumn:
Generally, they respect a word of honor from one military
      commander to another.
      Emir Galafre proposes to give hostages as proof of his hon-
      esty and trustworthiness:
       “If you suspect me of treacherous guile
       I shall let both my sons as hostages ride.
       No fortune so great will ransom their lives,
       you shall hang them both from a tree to die.”

           — The Coronation of Louis, XIX
        When delivering a message to a Saracen court, Franks
      should be prudent, however, because there is a limit to the
      Saracens’ respect of diplomatic immunity.
      Fortifications

        The Saracens are great builders. Their castles and fortresses
      are generally strong and much bigger than Frankish strongholds.
      Their cities, especially, often have high solid walls reinforced
      with many towers. In the countryside, the Saracens use a dense
      network of wooden guard towers to alert the surrounding villag-
      es and towns, making them difficult to surprise.
      Persians

      Names
      M
           en: Abdallaziz, Harun, Hishem, Jafar, Jamal, Mansur,
           Rashid, Sayid, Suleiman, Tarik, Yazid, Yusuf.
              Women: Asma, Dinazade, Halima, Layla,
      Sherazade, Sumaya.
      Appearance
        Persians resemble the Saracens in stature (–1 SIZ, +1
      DEX) and share the same other outward characteristics, though
      Persians are more handsome (+1 APP) with a copper tan, black
      curly hair, and deep brown eyes. Men wear a small pointy beard.
      They wear lose-fitting robes, turbans and ornamented curved
      daggers. Persian ladies wear ornamented dresses and a transpar-
      ent veil which covers at least the upper half of their face.
      Character

        The people from Persia form a tolerant and Just civilization.
      Like the Saracens, the Persian culture separates the private and
      public life of men and women (Chaste). Because of the eternal
      wars with Byzantium, many Persians Hate [Byzantines]. Their
      warriors are simply described as Valorous: “Persians are brave,
      trusting to the horse no less than to their skill with weapons.”
      — Ermold the Black.
        Unlike all other cultures (including Saracens), Persians do
      not drink wine nor any other alcoholic beverage (Temperate).
      Persians never look a foreign woman directly in the eyes.
rightColumn:
Skills
     All noblemen are educated, are proficient in Reading &
  Writing and have a certain knowledge of Languages and Eloquence,
  but their pagan nature leads them to follow many superstitions
  (Faerie Lore). Compared to the Franks, the Persians have far
  more knowledge in the domains of sciences, manufacturing tech-
  niques and healing (Chirurgery). Persians are merchants by nature
  and travel great distances by land or sea to reach foreign markets
  (Stewardship). Life in the city has familiarized them with the sub-
  tleties of administrative and political machinations (Intrigue).
  Relations with the Franks

     Even though contact is difficult, the Persians are more or less al-
  lied with the Franks against the Moors and Saracens, especially when
  Harun al-Rashid comes to power. Under King Pepin’s rule an em-
  bassy is sent to Baghdad, which returns in 768, together with Persian
  ambassadors and numerous presents. In 777, Persian ambassadors
  come to Charlemagne to negotiate an alliance against Marsile in ex-
  change for support and the protection of pilgrims in the Holy Land.
     From 797 on, a number of embassies are exchanged, this
  time looking for an alliance against the Byzantines. The caliph
  sends Charlemagne many fabulous presents, including a white
  elephant and a water-clock.
    The Persians brought the emperor an elephant, monkeys,
    balsam, nard, and various ointments, spices, perfumes,
    and different medicines to such an extent that the East
    seemed emptied and the West filled.
       — Notker, 2.8
     Negotiations between the Franks and the Persians are of-
  ten about the city of Jerusalem. Harun agrees to put it under
  Frankish overlordship, although the Persians maintain their mil-
  itary presence to protect the Christians against the Saracens.
    Harun: “I will give the Holy Land into Charlemagne’s
    power, and I will be the advocate over it. He himself,
    whenever it shall seem most opportune, may direct en-
    voys to me, and he will find me a most faithful steward of
    all the income of this very province.”
       — Notker, 2.9
  Chronology

    768 The first Frankish embassy to Persia returns.
    777 Persian envoys ask Charlemagne to attack the Moors.
    783 The Saracens capture Jerusalem.
    789–792 Frankish-Persian reconquest of Jerusalem.
    796 Two powerful Persian tribes fight each other in the Holy
      Lands.
    797 The second Frankish embassy is sent to Baghdad.
    801 Saracen invasion of Jerusalem.
    802 Third Frankish embassy to Baghdad.
    807 Fourth Frankish embassy to Baghdad.
    809 Death of Harun al-Rashid.

title: Territory and Nations
leftColumn:
Territory and Nations

        Persia: The lands of Persia lie in the fertile river valleys be-
      yond the Arabian desert, bordered in the east by the sheer, im-
      passable Zagros Mountains.
        Holy Lands: The land around the Holy City from the
      Mediterranean coast to the Jordan River is called the Holy Land
      by the Christians.
      Terrain Types
        The coastal areas and the cultivated valleys of the Tigris and
      the Euphrates are irrigated by an intricate system of canals. The
      rest of the Persian lands consist of sandy or stony deserts, some
      grassy plains and dry rocky hills and mountains.
      Climate

        Persia has very hot, dry summers and rather cold winters.
      Sand storms occasionally occur during the hot season.
      Travel

        Most voyagers take a boat following one of the great rivers.
      Land travel through the desert is done on camels, by ponies or
      mules in hilly or grassy terrain.
      Places of Interest
        Baghdad: The fabled home of the caliph is situated on the
      banks of the Tigris River. It is the commercial, scientific and political
      heart of Persia, and one of the biggest and richest cities in the world.
      In its center lies a peninsula surrounded by triple walls, named the
      Round City. It holds the luxuriously-decorated Great Temple, the
      caliph’s Golden Gate Palace with its emerald dome, the delicious
      Palace Gardens, and the residential quarter for the guards, senior
      officers and high noblemen. The Round City’s four gates are locked
      at night. Canals crisscross through Baghdad’s surrounding popular
      quarters, which are inhabited by merchants and artisans.
        Damascus: The City of Jasmine lies on the Great Road
      leading from the Mediterranean Sea to Baghdad. It is defended
      by a square citadel and a high city wall with seven gates. The
      Grand Temple, holding several Christian relics, and the Treasury
      Tower can be found on the central town square. The population
      is a mix of Christians, Jews, Persians and other peoples, such as
      Byzantine and Saracen traders. Once the capital of the caliphate,
      it is now the home of some Persian dissidents and rebels.
       Damascus is said to be one of the richest cities of the Le-
       vant, one of the most populous and splendid; it lies in a fer-
       tile, fruitful plain at seven days’ journey from Jerusalem;
       it is no less pleasing a spot in winter than in summer. A
       nearby hill conceals from it the first rays of the rising sun.
       Two crystal streams flow through the city, coursing down
       many channels to irrigate the countless gardens which are
       always in leaf, always in flower. There is enough rose-wa-
       ter to turn mill-wheels, and whoever walks through the
       streets smells fragrant odors issuing from every house.
           — Orlando Furioso, XVII
rightColumn:
Jerusalem: The Holy City is the center of the independent
  region called the Patriarchate of Jerusalem. The city is fortified by
  high stone walls and many towers. The center of Christianity holds
  many churches, including the Church of the Holy Sepulcher. The
  Caliph grants free access for Christian pilgrims, who come here to
  make generous donations to Christian holy places. Jerusalem holds
  a great annual market visited by Byzantine, Persian, Lombard and
  Jewish merchants. The latter bring back spices, silk, glassware and
  later even paper to Frankland.
    Four months the king stayed in Jerusalem.
    He and the twelve peers, the most exquisite escort,
    Spend their money lavishly, for Charlemagne is generous.
    They order the construction of a church, dedicated to St.
     Mary,
    Which the local population calls “Latina.”
       — Pilgrimage of Charlemagne, XII
     Tormont: This disputed fortified border town is held alter-
  nately by the Persians and the Saracens.

  Society

     The Persian empire is vast and immensely rich. It is gov-
  erned by a caliph, who is assisted in all daily business by a vizier
  and a court magician. In the cities, a qadi (judge) dispenses jus-
  tice in the caliph’s name, and street militias maintain law and
  order. Local noblemen hold the surrounding lands and access to
  sources of water. In return, they send the caliph knights and sol-
  diers in times of war.
     This enlightened people accepts and respects Christians and
  Jews, but they come to fear and hate the neighboring Saracens, with
  whom they are allied until the disastrous campaign against Rome in
  767. The Holy Land receives substantial financial support from the
  Persians, the Byzantines, and Charlemagne, who sends money for
  the construction of churches, hostelries and a library.
  Religion
     The Persian pagans worship the Sun. They pray together
  with their slaves, but they do not use books nor do they have
  priests. Some of them dance and chant in an enthralling fashion
  while praying.
  Daily Life and Economy
     Most Persians live close to a source of water, which they use
  to irrigate their fields. Other inhabited areas are the oases in the
  desert or the serails along the main caravan trails, where travelers
  and merchants spend time to rest and replenish their food and
  water supplies. Note that Persian food is very odd to Frankish
  taste and stomachs.
     The great Persian cities are supported by intensive irrigation
  agriculture. The trade in gold, horses, silk, spices and slaves is
  the prime source of wealth. Persian merchants have commercial
  relations with almost all known countries, including far Cathay
  and Sericane. Thanks to their far-flung, international contacts,
  the Persians have made significant scientific progress in many

      scholars and accomplished artists, and his court has become a
      major home of innovation in many areas, such as astrology, phar-
      macology, alchemy, medicine, and music.
      Warfare

        The Persians are eternally at war with the Byzantines. The
      backbone of the caliph’s army consists of light, very mobile cav-
      alry. The infantry is slow and not always reliable. Infantry ar-
      chers are used to harass the enemy until the horsemen charge or
      maneuver to outflank the enemy. The goal is often to reach the
      enemy camp in order to plunder it. The Persians’ favorite tactics
      are feigned retreats and nocturnal ambushes.
        The Persian Caliph flies a black banner and his soldiers
      wear black, apart from the troops defending Jerusalem, who
      wear white clothes.
      Standard Equipment
        Nobles: Byzantine scale armor, conical pointed helmet
      (9 points) and a small shield (4 points); sword or mace, lance,
      curved dagger; a courser or a camel.
        Footmen: Light or no armor (0 to 2 points) and a small shield
      (4 points); spear or javelin or compound bow, curved dagger.
      Code of Honor

        The feudalized Persians appreciate the noble code of
      knighthood as much as the Franks, which reinforces their
      friendship. Some particularly noble Persian knights even respect
      the ways of chivalry, like Carahue:
       “Just king,” says he, “good grace, hear me now!
       They took Ogier away from you, but lest no one
       Should believe I was involved in such a heinous act,
       I will constitute myself your prisoner and thus stay
       Until Ogier the Dane shall be delivered.”
       “What a chivalrous pagan!” say the Franks cheerfully.

           — Enfances Ogier
      Fortifications

        The coastal areas of the Holy Lands are defended by stone cas-
      tles and guard towers in order to prevent Byzantine or Saracen raids.
      The cities in the Persian heartland are always protected by high walls
      and dozens of stone towers. In the countryside, all oases are guarded
      by a high stone tower. Even the caravan serails are often fortified.

  Appearance
     The Romans are handsome (+1 APP), rather small (–1
  SIZ, –1 STR), dark-haired, often with an elegant but large nose.
  Men shave, and both sexes wear long robes, often white, and
  much jewelry.
  Character

     The Romans are Proud of their city and its prestigious
  history. They are always scheming (Deceitful) and forever con-
  cerned about food (Indulgent) and money (Selfish).
  Skills

     Due to their sophisticated education they speak well in pub-
  lic (Reading & Writing, Languages, Eloquence), and know their
  way around in a bureaucracy or at a senatorial meeting (Courtesy,
  Intrigue). Since Rome is the city of the Pope, the Christian dog-
  mas and religion have no secrets for them (Religion). Many se-
  nior Church members are members of the local aristocracy, so
  the Church looks at the Romans citizens with a particular kind
  of affection (Standing [Church]).
  Relations with the Franks
     Ever since the Pope anointed Pepin the Short and made the
  king and his descendants the official Protectors of Rome, the
  Franks have been unswervingly loyal allies of the Eternal City.
  Rome has been besieged by enemies more than once, and each
  time the Franks have come across the Alps to prevent the capture
  of the city.
  Chronology

    753 Sultan Corsuble besieges Rome.
    756 The Lombards attack the Pope in his city.
    767 The Saracens seize Rome, but the Frankish army comes
      to the Pope’s rescue and forces the pagans to retreat.
    774 Charlemagne conquers Lombardy, ratifies the
      Donation of Constantine, and visits the Pope.
    781 Emir Galafre besieges Rome. The siege is resolved by
      single combat between Count William and the giant
      Corsolt.
    799 Pope Leo is mutilated by his political adversaries.
    800 Charlemagne restores the order in Rome and crowns
      himself Emperor.
  Territory
     Rome is built on seven hills about 15 miles from the mouth
  of the Tiber River. King Pepin the Short donated the lands

title: Saxons and Frisians
leftColumn:
around Rome to the Pope in 754, creating the Papal States as
      an official autonomous region ruled by the Pope. The weather
      is generally nice, with hot summers and a clement winter. Many
      ancient roads lead to Rome, and ships sail in and out from the
      harbor of Portus daily. Inside the city, wide paved roads allow
      easy transport by cart or on horseback.
      Places of Interest
        Farfa: The richest and most important Benedictine abbey
      of Italy, situated north of Rome. It is famous for its illuminators
      and gold smiths.
        Naples: An ancient walled harbor town with a stone castle,
      a cathedral and an aqueduct.
        Rome: Rome is the most ancient, and one of the largest, cit-
      ies of Western Europe, though not as big as it used to be. Many
      houses are abandoned or in ruins, as are many of the ancient
      buildings such as the Coliseum. The city has double walls and
      stone guard towers. The Pope resides in the Lateran Palace on the
      Caelian Hill in the city, next to the cathedral of the Holy Savior
      and the Baptistery of Saint John. The Vatican Palace is on Vatican
      Hill, outside the walls across the Tiber, next to St. Peter’s Basilica.
      Society

        The Pope must be elected from the Roman aristocracy.
      This practice has led to the creation of numerous local factions,
      which each work for the advancement of their members within
      the clerical and political organization of Rome.
      Religion
        Naturally, all Romans are fervent Christians.

      Family and Settlements
        Of Roman origin, the rich papal cities are walled and often
      have paved streets, bath houses and various Roman monuments.
      Economy

        Apart from the traditional economic functions of a great
      city, the most important source of income is the Church. The
      tithe brings in good money, as do the gifts of pilgrims and am-
      bassadors seeking the favor of the Roman pontiff. In addition,
      the numerous cathedrals and abandoned tombs draw a lot of
      relic collectors from all over the West, and some unscrupulous
      Romans make a substantial living out of the relic trade.
      Warfare

        The Pope maintains a permanent city guard and a fleet to
      ward off Saracen pirates and raiders. Most of the warriors are
      Roman citizens, but in times of need Christian mercenaries are
      hired.
      Standard Equipment
        Equites (Knights): Scale armor and an iron helmet (10
      points), wooden shield (6 points); sword, spear, dagger; charger
rightColumn:
and rouncy (note that Roman knights wear a cross on their hel-
  met, instead of plumes).
     Footmen: Cuirbouilli armor and iron helmet (7 points),
  large shield (7 points); short sword, spear, dagger.
  Code of Honor

     Roman knights often swear oaths on God. They have a very
  acute sense of personal Honor and can be quite touchy and easily
  provoked.
  Saxons    and  Frisians

  T
      he Saxons live in the northern part of Germania, while
      the Frisians inhabit the coast of the North Sea from the
      duchy of Flanders-Artois to Denmark. Apart from the
  Frisians, there are three Saxon tribes: the Westphalians, the
  Angarians and the Eastphalians.
  Names
     Men: Abbion, Adalbrecht, Bernlef, Beorn, Cunrad,
  Grimbold, Hildebrand, Oswin, Sigfrid, Widukind, Wulfstan.
     Women: Altrude, Gudrun, Gunhild, Hildegard, Ingeborg,
  Walda.
  Appearance

     The Saxons are rather clumsy (–1 DEX) and ugly (–1
  APP) but, like the Danes, they are strong (+1 STR) and tall (+1
  SIZ). They are blue-eyed and have blond hair with wild beards.
  Saxons wear golden necklaces (torcs) as status symbols.
  Character
     The Saxons are sinful and evil devil-worshipers, who have
  no honor (Arbitrary). These traitorous barbarians are Deceitful,
  and very Vengeful and Cruel.
    The Saxons are ferocious by nature. They are much given
    to devil worship and they are hostile to our religion. They
    think it no dishonor to violate and transgress the laws
    of God and man. They are always willing to break the
    promises they make. Hardly a day passes without some
    incident which breaks the peace. Murder, robbery and
    arson are of constant occurrence.
       — Einhard

  Skills
     Frisian merchants are cunning tricksters (Stewardship).
  They know the law and have a very keen legal mind:
    Beware of the Frisians, my son. Let me tell you the tale
    of the unwary Frankish merchant who exchanged a gold
    torque for as much dust as a Frisian could hold in his
    clothes. The man gathered dust everywhere, scattered it
    over a large area of land, and then loudly proclaimed it
    to be his!
       — Res Gestae Saxonicae

title: Relations with the Franks
leftColumn:
Relations with the Franks

        The Saxons are the Franks’ most intimate and bitter ene-
      mies. Charles Martel and Pepin the Short both organized several
      punitive raids into Saxony, but they never aimed to conquer the
      land. Two holy oaks were destroyed: one at Geismar, the other
      near Fritzlar, in 723.
        Allied to the Danes, the Saxons refuse to pay homage and
      regularly raid Austrasia and Thuringia. Very early in his reign
      Charlemagne decides to conquer and convert his fierce neigh-
      bors. “War was duly declared on them. It was waged with immense
      hatred on both sides.” — Einhard
        Slowly, the Franks take a physical and spiritual hold on
      Saxony. Missionaries build churches and the lands of its deport-
      ed inhabitants are given to Frankish nobles or newly appointed
      Saxon counts. Paradoxically, the Saxon nobles (especially ladies)
      admire the refined Frankish court life. Indeed, several Saxon
      leaders rally to the Frankish cause at one time or another, for
      they are caught in a paradox: to effectively resist their Frankish
      neighbors, they must adopt the superior customs of feudalism
      and knighthood; but by doing so they lose the very things they
      are fighting for: their cultural identity and independence. After

     The ground is covered with glacial debris, sand, and peat
  bogs. The landscape is dominated by rivers and forests. The
  Saxon homeland is mostly covered with impenetrable hilly for-
  ests and swamps. In fact, the only areas not naturally forested are
  the high mountains, bogs, and coastal marshes.
     Frisia is the western coastal area, characterized by wide,
  poorly-drained salt marshes covered with peat, cut by meander-
  ing creeks and tidal inlets, bays and river estuaries. Off the coast
  lie many sand banks and islands.
  Climate
     In the coastal areas the climate is rather mild, but the hin-
  terland knows a cold and inhospitable dark season, when life
  seems almost to come to a standstill.

  Travel
     The easiest way to travel in Saxony is to navigate along
  rivers, lakes, or the coast. Riding through light forests is slow-
  er, because of the numerous impenetrable marshes and dense
  forests which dot the landscape. There are no bridges across
  the wild rivers, which have to be forded, preferably on horse-
  back or in carts.

  boats. They use smaller flatboats to cross the marshy plains on
  the mainland.

segments.text: Relations with the Franks

The Saxons are the Franks’ most intimate and bitter ene-
      mies. Charles Martel and Pepin the Short both organized several
      punitive raids into Saxony, but they never aimed to conquer the
      land. Two holy oaks were destroyed: one at Geismar, the other
      near Fritzlar, in 723.
        Allied to the Danes, the Saxons refuse to pay homage and
      regularly raid Austrasia and Thuringia. Very early in his reign
      Charlemagne decides to conquer and convert his fierce neigh-
      bors. “War was duly declared on them. It was waged with immense
      hatred on both sides.” — Einhard
        Slowly, the Franks take a physical and spiritual hold on
      Saxony. Missionaries build churches and the lands of its deport-
      ed inhabitants are given to Frankish nobles or newly appointed
      Saxon counts. Paradoxically, the Saxon nobles (especially ladies)
      admire the refined Frankish court life. Indeed, several Saxon
      leaders rally to the Frankish cause at one time or another, for
      they are caught in a paradox: to effectively resist their Frankish
      neighbors, they must adopt the superior customs of feudalism
      and knighthood; but by doing so they lose the very things they
      are fighting for: their cultural identity and independence. After
      long years of bloody warfare, the Saxons are finally converted
      and assimilated, often becoming Charlemagne’s most loyal vas-
      sals. “United with the Franks, the Saxons came to form with them
      a single people.” — Einhard

title: Society
leftColumn:
Their custom was to hold a general meeting once a year in
       the center of Saxony near the river Weser at a place called
       Marklo. There all the satraps (chiefs) used to gather to-
       gether and they were joined by twelve noblemen from
       each clan with as many freemen and serfs. There they
       confirmed the laws, gave judgment on outstanding cas-
       es and by common consent drew up plans for the coming
       year on which they could act either in peace or war.
           — Vita Lebuini Antiqua
      Society

        Each tribe is divided into independent clans. Each individu-
      al Saxon belongs to one of three castes: rich nobles (Edhilingui),
      freemen (Frilingi), or prisoner-slaves (Lazzi).
       This people is entirely divided into three orders: there are
       those who are called in their languages edhilingui, frilingi
       and lazzi. In our tongue that is nobles, freemen and serfs.
           — Nithard
        Edhilingui are essentially rich freemen who possess a
      wooden stronghold, often on a hilltop. They pay warriors
      (Hearthguards) in their service. The word “Saxon” means “war-
      rior of a war-band” (much like the word Viking). Scops, respect-
      ed harpists (a sort of bard, like the Danish skalds), are the living
      memory of the tribe and live either at their chief’s court or wan-
      der around freely. They inspire warriors before battle.
        Land cannot be held as a private property, so free Saxons
      can settle wherever they like. There is no central authority
      with which the Franks can negotiate lasting treaties, for the
      Saxons are divided into numerous autonomous clans. Clan
      leaders gather every year at the Allthing, somewhere in the
      forest near Marklo. Still, internal tribal cohesion is often
      weak due to frequent internal struggles between the freemen
      and the rich nobles. The latter sometimes gravitate towards
      the Franks, because they need alliances against each other
      and against the local freemen, who are often eager to revolt
      against their leaders. So Saxon nobles are often pro-Frankish
      and convert more easily, seeing the benefits of Christianity
      and feudalism, while the opposite is true for the frilingi, who
      are often afraid of their leader converting to Christianity and
      forcing them to do the same, consequently revolting against
      their own chiefs.
      Religion
        Their main gods are Wotan (magic, knowledge), Donar
      (war, home) and Saxnot (the dead). They pray near shrines,
      temples and idols, but most of all to holy trees, like the Irminsul,
      which are used for blood sacrifices (mostly slaves and prisoners
      of war), and rich votive offerings which they bury under the
      roots. They ask their gods for help and their shamans or scops
      practice rituals of divination and soothsaying.
        Saxons cremate their dead together with personal belong-
      ings (swords, horses, and gold). Since the dead are sacred, no
      Saxon will ever take something from a Saxon burial mound.
rightColumn:
Under Charles Martel, the chief missionary was Boniface,
  who converted many Frisians before being slain by them in 754.
  Then Lebuin (died 776) tries to convert the Saxons, and later
  Abbot Sturm (died 799) takes over.
    They came back to their pagan customs like a dog returns
    to its vomit!
       — Einhard
     Exasperated by their faithlessness, Charlemagne decides to
  convert the Saxons at all cost: “Who have been given over to de-
  mons since the beginning of time, will enter into the sweet yoke of
  Christ.” Even after their forced conversion, the Saxons remain
  half pagan, because the local Christian priests are poorly educat-
  ed. All Frankish missionary outposts are heavily fortified.
  Daily Life and Economy

     Saxons are a semi-nomadic people and have no cities. Their
  villages are isolated from each other by forests and valleys, which
  are partly covered with peat bogs. Saxons depend on agriculture
  and the rearing of horses. The grassy valleys are used for cattle
  grazing. Most temporary settlements can be found along the rivers
  Elbe and Weser, where the Saxons live in wooden stable-houses.
  Whenever food shortages occur, the men raid neighboring re-
  gions, usually the agriculturally more developed Franks or Slavs.
     The Frisians live in the coastal marshes, either in small har-
  bor villages with a long street parallel to the coast or navigable
  waterway, or on artificial, flat-topped clay mounds. Their wick-
  erwork houses are daubed with clay to make them waterproof.
  They fish, raise cattle, horses and sheep on the nearby salt marsh-
  es, and grow grain on the higher marsh land.
     Saxons speak a Germanic language very similar to Frankish.
  They often give alliterative names to their children. Most Saxons
  are illiterate; only their shamans use runes to carve their secret
  formulas on stones or on pieces of wood, which they strap to
  a man’s arm with leather. Runes are mainly used as safeguards
  against illness, dangers and bad luck.
     Saxony is poorly developed and the economy is based on
  cattle breeding rather than on arable farming. Since to Saxons
  land cannot be individually owned, a man’s wealth is measured
  by his livestock. Instead of coins, they use small pieces of hacked
  silver like the Danes. Nobles trade by bartering agricultural pro-
  duce or luxury items like swords, jewelry or linen gowns. The
  only things they produce for trade are salt and ore. Frankish mer-
  chants almost never venture into Saxony.
     In contrast to inland Saxons, the Frisians have a coin-based
  currency system. They are renowned merchants (or pirates), and
  possess a considerable fleet based at Dorestad harbor. They trade
  widely with the British Isles, Scandinavia, the Baltic and along
  the rivers into the mainland all the way down to Spain and Italy.
  Warfare
     The Saxons fight almost exclusively as infantry, because the
  dense forests doesn’t really favor mounted combat. Saxons often use
  shield walls, and they dig hidden ditches to disrupt enemy cavalry.

  waterway, or on artificial, flat-topped clay mounds. Their wick-
  erwork houses are daubed with clay to make them waterproof.
  They fish, raise cattle, horses and sheep on the nearby salt marsh-
  es, and grow grain on the higher marsh land.
     Saxons speak a Germanic language very similar to Frankish.
  They often give alliterative names to their children. Most Saxons
  are illiterate; only their shamans use runes to carve their secret
  formulas on stones or on pieces of wood, which they strap to
  a man’s arm with leather. Runes are mainly used as safeguards
  against illness, dangers and bad luck.
     Saxony is poorly developed and the economy is based on
  cattle breeding rather than on arable farming. Since to Saxons
  land cannot be individually owned, a man’s wealth is measured
  by his livestock. Instead of coins, they use small pieces of hacked
  silver like the Danes. Nobles trade by bartering agricultural pro-
  duce or luxury items like swords, jewelry or linen gowns. The
  only things they produce for trade are salt and ore. Frankish mer-
  chants almost never venture into Saxony.
     In contrast to inland Saxons, the Frisians have a coin-based
  currency system. They are renowned merchants (or pirates), and
  possess a considerable fleet based at Dorestad harbor. They trade
  widely with the British Isles, Scandinavia, the Baltic and along
  the rivers into the mainland all the way down to Spain and Italy.
  Warfare
     The Saxons fight almost exclusively as infantry, because the
  dense forests doesn’t really favor mounted combat. Saxons often use
  shield walls, and they dig hidden ditches to disrupt enemy cavalry.

       The Old Saxons have no king but only a number of sa-

      or rouncy.

      axe or sword, bow, dagger.
      Code of Honor
        Saxon warriors have no knightly honor, but they respect the
      traditions of hospitality. Generally, the only promises they keep
      are the ones they swear to their pagan gods. They do not hesitate
      to massacre women and children, and seem to delight in burning
      churches and killing monks and priests. However, sooner or later
      Saxon chiefs adopt the noble customs of knighthood.
      Fortifications

        Rich nobles often have small wooden ring forts on hilltops.
      The Saxons no longer build stone castles.

Relations with the Franks

    “What do these little frogs matter to me? I could carry
    seven, eight or nine of them about strung on my lance
    muttering I don’t know what! It’s a shame that our lord
    king and we should weary ourselves killing such worms!”
       — Notker the Stammerer, 12
     The different Slavic tribes are constantly warring on each
  other, and these divisions are an opportunity exploited by
  Charlemagne, who sometimes uses one tribe to attack anoth-
  er. Conquered Slav tribes are either completely annihilated, or
  made subservient to a newly appointed local leader. Once con-
  verted, these tribes often become allies against the pagan Saxons.
  Chronology
    772 Duke Tassilo of Bavaria conquers Carinthia.

    780 The Obodrites become Frankish allies. The Franks start
      building missionary outposts.
    789 Charlemagne subdues the Wiltzi.
    796 The Slavs ally with the Franks against the Avars.
    804 Several Slav tribes submit to the Franks, but others rebel
      against Charlemagne’s authority.
    805–811 The Franks defeat the Slavs and their Danish and
      Hunnic allies. Several Slav kings die in battle.
  Territory

     The lands of the Slavs, or Slavonia, stretches out from the
  northern banks of the Danube River across the steppe plains of
  eastern Europe between Saxony and Byzantium. Note that most
  of the slaves in the Hunnic lands of the Avars and the Bulgars
  are Slavs.
  Terrain Types
     Slavonia is mostly forested hills or steppe plains.
  Climate

     The continental climate is characterized by very cold win-
  ters, during which daily life comes to a virtual standstill.
  Travel
     The Slavs use boats to navigate along rivers, mainly for local
  trade. The frequent rapids are negotiated by small, shallow-draft
  boats, while larger vessels are carried overland.
     To escape from attacks, desperate Slavs sometimes march
  through dense, trackless forest where only they know the way.
  Fleeing on the plains is not an option, since they have very
  few horses.

  Places of Interest
     Magdeburg: A medium wooden fortress founded by
  Charlemagne (805) in the land of the Sorbs.

title: Society
leftColumn:
Society

        The Slavs are divided into patriarchal clans, linked into five
      different tribes: the Sorbs, the Obodrites, the Wilzi, the Czechs,
      and the Croats. There is little to no central power, as the tribes
      are as much rivals as a single people. The local chiefs dwell in cir-
      cular wooden citadels, surrounded by open farming settlements.
      In their fortified homes, these nobles keep a warrior retinue
      called a druzhina. Their main function is to collect tribute and
      punish those who oppose their leader. The smaller settlements
      are governed by the tribe elders.
      Religion
        The pagan Slavs worship a polytheistic pantheon, including
      such deities as Perun (the main god, of storms, lightning and oak
      trees), Svarog (the sun, war, fertility), Stribog (hunting, winds),
      Khors (cattle) and Mokosh (women, the household). The Slavs
      pray in open-air cult places with a stone hearth and wooden stat-
      ues on high river banks, surrounded by a ring ditch.
        Nobles are interred in underground catacombs inside hills,
      while commoners are usually cremated on funeral pyres. When a
      chief dies, his family and serfs are also killed and cremated.
        Slavs believe that spirits and demons live near crossroads,
      rivers, springs, trees, rocks or on the edges of bogs and ponds, as
      well as deep inside forests. The Slavs make offerings or animal
      sacrifices to keep them at bay. Friendly home spirits, like ances-
      tors, help the priests by predicting the future, while malevolent
      demons (small, naked, dark-skinned creatures with extra fingers)
      have the ability to light fires, become invisible and cause illness.
        Vila are strong, beautiful, naked nymphs or faeries armed
      with bows, who live near springs, in caves or under trees or rocks.
      They dance on hilltops at night and are able to transform into
      swans, snakes, horses, wolves or whirlwinds. The Faerie King
      lives in the deep forest near a sacred oak. He is generally hostile
      to humans and sometimes takes on the form of a giant wolf, owl
      or whirlwind.
        Under Frankish military pressure, some tribes are forced to
      convert to Christianity.
      Daily Life and Economy
        Like the neighboring Saxons, the Slavs have no real cities.
      They live primarily as fishermen, cattle-raising herdsmen, or
      farmers, and trade with Saxons, Franks and Byzantines along
      the great navigable rivers and along the coasts. Their armed
      merchants travel in groups and use hacksilver, pelts and pieces of
      cloth as means of payment. In the areas under Hunnic control,
      the Slavs pay silver and furs as a tribute to their overlords.
        They build their villages on steep promontories or in boggy
      places difficult to access. Undefended rural settlements are often
      near navigable rivers or a lake, giving villagers a way to escape in
      case of attack. Larger trading villages are surrounded by timber
      walls, earthen ramparts and ditches, with several entrances.
        All men are shaved bald except for a single thin tail at the
      back. For women, hairstyle indicates their social position, age

and marital status. Nobles practice polygamy. Chiefs welcome
  their important guests by taking a sauna together.
  Warfare

     Internal strife, small-scale raids and ambushes are daily
  bread to the Slavs. A typical warrior band consists of around 200
  warriors. They raid primarily to enhance wealth and community
  prestige for the leader and his druzhina, rather than to conquer.
     Slavs usually use ambushes, sudden attacks and tricks, often
  during the night. They tend not to fight in an organized fashion,
  nor do they like to fight in the open, but rather prefer difficult
  swampy grounds where heavy armored knights are at a disadvan-
  tage. Success against the Slavs depends mainly on speed, denying
  the targeted tribe time to organize its defenses.
     Their lack of military unity and strength makes them
  easy victims. Slav prisoners are often used as slave laborers by
  the Frankish army, deported into Frankland, or sold. Slavs
  themselves do not take slaves, but they do take war prisoners.
  However, they do not keep these indefinitely, but let them go
  after a certain period of time and payment of ransom.
  Standard Equipment
     Nobles: Leather armor and metal helmet (6 points), wood-
  en shield (6 points); sword, dagger; pony or rouncy.
     Footmen: Padded armor (2 points), wooden shield (6
  points); spear, axe, sling or bow, dagger.
  Code of Honor

     Warriors are loyal to their chief as long as he sustains them.
  They do not follow the customs of civilized warriors.
  Fortifications
     The strongholds serve as homes for tribal chiefs and as ref-
  uges for the local population. They are usually built on hilltops
  and fortified with limestone ramparts or compact earthen ring-
  works, with an access to fresh water. The clan leaders each have
  their own limestone fortress. These rather weak strongholds are
  built for prestige as much as any military purpose.
     The Slavs’ best defense is the virgin forest, which acts as an
  impenetrable buffer-zone. Sometimes, they build linear earthworks
  between forests and marshes for archers to cover a hasty retreat.

  However, they do not keep these indefinitely, but let them go
  after a certain period of time and payment of ransom.
  Standard Equipment
     Nobles: Leather armor and metal helmet (6 points), wood-
  en shield (6 points); sword, dagger; pony or rouncy.
     Footmen: Padded armor (2 points), wooden shield (6
  points); spear, axe, sling or bow, dagger.
  Code of Honor

Warriors are loyal to their chief as long as he sustains them.
  They do not follow the customs of civilized warriors.
  Fortifications
     The strongholds serve as homes for tribal chiefs and as ref-
  uges for the local population. They are usually built on hilltops
  and fortified with limestone ramparts or compact earthen ring-
  works, with an access to fresh water. The clan leaders each have
  their own limestone fortress. These rather weak strongholds are
  built for prestige as much as any military purpose.
     The Slavs’ best defense is the virgin forest, which acts as an
  impenetrable buffer-zone. Sometimes, they build linear earthworks
  between forests and marshes for archers to cover a hasty retreat.

        Gedeon, Floris, Hamon, Milo, Nimfri, Nizezi, Roda,

     Women: Adosinda, Blancheflour, Dodila, Esclarmunda,
  Froilubia, Gosvintha, Guibourc, Hilduara, Oriabel, Radegonda,
  Sybil.

title: Territories and Nations
leftColumn:
Appearance
        The Visigoths are slightly shorter than Franks (–1 SIZ) and
      usually have dark hair. The clothes worn by men and women
      differ little from the Gascon and Frankish styles, but Visigothic
      men have beards.
      Character

        The Visigoths are an easy-going, open-minded and Modest
      people.
      Skills

        Even though they live in a rather urban and mercantile cul-
      ture (Stewardship, Intrigue), the Visigoths are excellent horse-
      men (Horsemanship). The ethnic blend of their coastal towns
      contributes favorably to their Languages.
      Relations with the Franks

        Almost all of Provence is still under Moorish control in
      767. The Franks wholly reconquered Septimania in 754, and
      the independent Christian kingdom of Asturias has become
      their loyal ally against the Moors. The blood line of the Frankish
      kings and that of the Asturias have become mingled since the
      marriage of Pepin the Short and the Asturian Princess Bertrada
      Broadfoot, daughter of Floris and Blancheflour.
      Chronology (Provence, Septimania, Spanish March)
       714 The Saracens conquer the Iberian Peninsula.
       725 The Saracens conquer Septimania and Provence, taking
          captive many knights, who are sold as slaves.
       739 Partial liberation of Aquitaine by Charles Martel.
       754 Pepin the Short takes Narbonne with the help of the
          Lombards and the local nobility, completing the liber-
          ation of Septimania.
       776 Tiebaut besieges Narbonne.
       788 Emir Hisham raids Septimania.
       790 William Shortnose captures Nîmes.
       791 William Shortnose captures Orange.
       793 Battle of the Archant, where Vivien dies.
       801 The Franks capture Barcelona.
       803 Charlemagne creates the Spanish March which contains
          Septimania, Provence and the territories conquered
          in northern Spain. William Shortnose becomes its
          marquis.

       730 King Pelagius of Asturias discovers the holy bones of
          Saint James the Great in Santiago de Compostela, which
          attracts many Christian pilgrims.
       768 King Fruela assassinated.
       771 Charlemagne affirms Aurelio as the King of Asturias.
       774 King Aurelio succeeded by Silo.

      the throne of Asturias. Prince Alphonso II flees to the
      Basque Country.
    789 At Mauregato’s death, the monk Bermudo is elected

    791 Bermudo, defeated by the Saracens, abdicates. He is suc-
      ceeded by Alphonso II.
    798 Alphonso conquers Luiserna.
    813 Death of Alphonso. His son-in-law Hugo the Orphan
      becomes the King of Asturias.
  Territories and Nations
     Septimania: Also called the Narbonnaise (the region
  around Narbonne), it extends to Beziers and the Rhone in the
  east, the Black Hills of Carcassonne in the north, the Basque
  Pyrenees in the west, and the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean to
  the south. The most important cities are Béziers, Carcassonne,
  Nîmes and the capital Narbonne.
     Provence: This nominally Frankish region is under Saracen
  control at the start of Charlemagne’s reign. Provence stretches
  out in the Rhone valley south of Lyon to the Alps in the east
  and the Rhone in the west. Its major cities are Arles, Nîmes and
  Orange.
     Asturias: This poor and isolated Christian kingdom is sit-
  uated north of the River Douro, in the north-western part of
  Spain. Its capital is Oviedo. The kingdom is divided into 4 re-
  gions: Castilia (abandoned by the Moors), Galicia (annexed by
  Alphonso II in 792), Cantabria, and Leon.
     Emirate of Cordoba: Founded on the ancient Visigothic
  Kingdom, the Saracen emirate is still largely inhabited by
  Visigoths, especially the northern Tarraconensis region.
  Terrain Types
     Most of the Visigothic lands are coastal hills or mountains,
  with green river valleys surrounded by forested slopes and pine-
  grown plateaus.
     The Mediterranean climate produces hot and rather dry
  summers, and temperate winters. Asturias is a bit drier and
  windier.
  Places of Interest (Asturias, Northern Spain)

     For the places of Septimania and Provence, see Chapter 14:
  Frankland.
     Bile [Bilbao]: A rich Asturian city on the road to
  Compostela.
     Burgos: Charlemagne liberates this town, situated on the
  Douro River, from Moorish occupation in 771 and gives it to
  the King of Asturias with its city walls, castle and cathedral still
  intact.
     Oviedo: This cathedral town is the capital of Asturias. The
  kings try to improve the city’s defenses with a medium stone roy-
  al castle and city walls.
